docs.title: Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Mini Review
docs.text:
I used to use Google Pixel Buds, but then I went through 3 pairs of those, because they weren't very durable / I was clumsy in two ways:

  1. Occasionally, I would drop one on the ground and after a few times the audio would just stop working in the ear bud.
  2. After earwax had built up on the buds, I would clean them with a tooth pick and micro-fibre cloth and during the cleaning process, they would break.

So I started investigating for a new set of wireless earphones (not headphones), and landed on the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Mini. Here's how I got there and my review so far.

docs.title: My requirements
docs.text:
...for wireless earphones.

  • Use for running and every-day listening.
  • Fit securely on or in my ears.
  • Connect with multiple devices, but mainly Android and a Garmin running watch (so basically: connect via Bluetooth)
  • Have a decent battery life (1 day or more, ideally a few days at least).
  • Charge via replaceable battery or via USB-C.
  • Have some kind of noise pass-through, or able to turn off noise-cancelling, to allow for hearing traffic / things around me whilst using them.
  • Have decent audio - not audiophile quality, or even excellent audio, just... acceptable - since I'll be running / commuting and want to hear what's around me anyway, so the audio quality is already massively affected by that.
  • Have a microphone, that is decent sounding.
  • Good / intuitive controls for volume and play/pausing audio.
  • Be durable.
  • Be repairable (be able to take apart, replace battery, replace parts etc.)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
...at the time of buying:

  • Fairbuds by Fairphone
    • Repairable (replaceable battery)
    • Saw reviews online and read the RTings review that showed decent audio and controls, but had mixed microphone quality, poor comfort and a very low battery life (5 hours).
    • I already own a Fairphone, so I would expect good integration.
    • Bluetooth connectivity.
    • Seemed to sit quite far out the ear, which looked odd but also did not inspire confidence that they would stay in place.
  • A OpenRun Pro 2 Mini by Shokz
    • Audio pass-through is part of the design (bone conduction rather than in-ear).
    • Decent audio quality (My friend had a OpenRun 1st generation, and it sounded fine, and the OpenRun Pro 2 had actual speakers added for improved audio quality).
    • Hooked over ears seemed more secure than in-ears, especially for running.
    • Thinking the Mini because I wanted a closer fit to my head (I have a big head so the Mini might have been too small, but trying on the normal size, I found it too big for me, so the Mini seems good).
    • Designed for running, so I would expect better water resistance / sweat proofing. They are "sweatproof": IP55 rated.
    • Not that repairable (no easily replaceable battery, but given the only option WITH a replaceable battery (that I could find) was the Fairbuds... then I can't really fulfil this requirement without the Fairbuds).
    • Good long battery life (9-12 hour), and charging via standard USB-C (not the Shokz proprietary connector as on other models).
    • Intuitive controls (volume buttons and an action button for play/pause/skip-track/back-track)

So, I went for the OpenRun Pro 2 Mini by Shokz!

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
It's pretty good!

The listening experience was a little odd at first because I could clearly hear audio and my surroundings, but I got used to it.

Wearing the device also felt odd (hooked over ears and gently pressing in just in front of my ears), but I got used to that too, and now I sometimes forget that I'm wearing them. The Mini was a good decision though, it's a closer fit to my head whilst not being too snug, but close enough that it doesn't catch on a collar or on things when I rest my head against something.

Seems durable (not broken yet), though the volume switches sometimes don't work and just spam "Battery High" in my ears over and over again.

I like the bone-conduction, though I do sometimes miss the "block out" that in-ear earphones and headphones provide either naturally or with noise-cancelling... but in those cases I'm usually in a static location, so then I just plug in some wired in-ear earphones (no battery, no bluetooth, just pure plug-in-cable-and-it-works goodness) or use headphones.

I look a little odd, in that the two black "speakers" make me look like I've got a sideburns.

docs.title: Signal Chat Backups
docs.text:
The Signal messaging app is a great messaging app for secure messaging.

It provides a way to create backups of the signal chats that you have with others, through the Chat backups feature.

docs.title: The issue with chat backups
docs.text:
These backups are only stored locally (on the device) and backing up to a remote location (a file server or Cloud storage solution) is not supported - see the Signal Support documentation.

This means that of your device gets lost, stolen, broken or corrupted, all your messages will be lost. For security, this is quite decent, and means that no one will be able to get access to those messages... not even you! However, for user experience, this kinda sucks.

If we want to save them, then we need to back up those backup files to a remote location such as a file server or cloud storage solution - like Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive or Dropbox.

Signal recently announced a new feature (still in beta) called "Signal Secure Backups".

It looks like it is Signal's own solution for remotely storing backups:

  • Backups are free for all text messages and the last 45 days of media.
  • A paid option is available for storing everything (up to 100 GB), at $1.99 / month.

It doesn't seem to provide an option for backing up any other storage provider other that Signal's own servers - I'm guessing they're doing that for security reasons, but it's not great for consumer choice (smells like vendor lock-in). It might be that this is just the best option in the end.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before digging into the solutions, it's helpful to understand the solution requirements:

  • Work on Android
  • Store chat backups in Google Drive (Android leads to Google products leads to Google Drive)
  • Simple to set up the backup
  • Ideally free, but I'd pay a small amount for an app to backups / syncs for me.
    • I'm not paying for a subscription though, as I already pay for Google Drive for storage, I don't want to also pay a subscription just for syncing some files.
  • Minimal or no advertisements (definitely no adverts if I pay for the app)
  • Acceptable intrusions
    • Minimal or zero impact my battery life (don't need it always running, I just need a backup to be uploaded in the night after the Chat backup is run).
    • Notification when the backup is done or failed (definitely if it failed).
    • Only asks for the permissions it needs (folder access on device, folder access in Google Drive) and nothing more.
    • Minimal or No gathering of data, and no sharing with 3rd parties (it's just a backup sync, I don't want to hand over my personal data for that, especially if they're going to then share that data with 3rd parties).

docs.title: Backing up the backups
docs.text:
From my digging, there are two options available to do this:

  • Autosync by MetaCtrl
  • Tasker by joaomgcd - though I didn't actually try this option, only read the Google Play app description.

Though BOTH options require one-time payment for long term use. Having tried Autosync, it also requires a lot of permissions and bypassing battery optimization settings, which I wouldn't be surprised if Tasker also required these.

You can find my full investigation below:

docs.title: Native Android feature?
docs.text:
Short answer: No.

Looking in Settings > System > Backup provides options for backing up Android things. The options are:

  • Apps (no sub-options)
  • Photos and videos (selecting opens Google Photos)
    • Backup quality
    • Mobile data usage
    • Back up device folders (only a limited list that doesn't include Signal, and would only back up photos & videos)
    • Back up Locked Folder
  • SMS and MMS messages (no sub-options)
  • Call history (no sub-options)
  • Device settings (no sub-options)
  • Google Account data (selecting opens a sub-menu)
    • List of Google apps for backup, none of which are Signal (obviously - it's not a Google app) or the Files app ( which is a Google app) for backing up files.

So, no ability to back up or sync device folders anywhere (not even to Google Drive).

docs.title: Files app feature?
docs.text:
I'm using the Files by Google app.

Short answer: No, but there is a useful Back up to Google Drive feature for backing up individual files manually.

There's no backup options in Settings.

If I go into Internal Storage and select my signal backup folder, there are no backup options but there are the following relevant options:

  • A Copy to option for copying files from one place to another, but not to a remote location.
  • A Quick Share option but that's just for copying to nearby devices.

If I go into Internal Storage, and into the signal backup folder, and select my latest signal backup, there are the following relevant options:

  • A Share option that opens up the Android share menu - which could be used to manually upload the file to Google Drive, but nothing automatically at a certain time.
  • A Copy to option for copying files from one place to another, but not to a remote location.
  • A Back up to Google Drive option for backing up files - which could be used manually to back up the file to Google Drive, in a nice way that is in the "background" - but sadly does not provide a way to automatically do backups at a specific time each day.

docs.title: Google Drive feature?
docs.text:
Short answer: No.

In the menu there is an Uploads menu that just shows current uploads (nothing to be able to configure a regular upload).

In Settings there is a Backup and reset option, but that just takes you to the Android backup settings, which proved not helpful. There's no other relevant options in Settings.

Pressing the big + button allows us to create an Upload, but not a automatic regular upload for doing automatic backups.

docs.title: A dedicated app for backups?
docs.text:
Unix philosophy #1: Make each program do one thing well.

What if we had an app that just did backups really well. Looking at the Google Play Store, this is what's available:

  • Swift Backup by SwiftApps.org.
  • Autosync (or other related apps) by MetaCtrl.
  • My Backup Pro by Rerware, LLC.
  • All Backup & Restore by SuriDevs.

other backup apps seemed to either want to (a) backup to their cloud storage and not Google Drive, or (b) backup specific things like SMS messages or APKs (Apps).

docs.title: Swift Backup
docs.text:
By SwiftApps.org. Short answer: No.

  • ❌ Only allows for backing up apps, messages and call logs
  • ℹ️ Free manual backups (of the above), requires payment for automatic backups - though it has a Lifetime plan for 159kr.
  • ⚠️ Requires "All files access" - bit much, could be using the Storage Access Framework to only give access to specific files or directories.
    • (Incidentally, check which apps have this access: Settings > Apps > Special app access > All files access. It's a bit annoying it's not available in the Permissions list for each App in Settings.)
  • ✅ No account needed with Swift Backup service, which is nice.
  • ✅ Good simple Android design.
  • ✅ No sharing of data with 3rd parties.
  • ⚠️ Some data collected (Personal Info, App info, and performance)
  • ℹ️ Support for more advanced features, for phones that are rooted (which mine isn't).

docs.title: Autosync
docs.text:
By MetaCtrl. Short answer: Mostly yes, but requires payment for long-term use and requires some sacrifices on non-functional requirements (security, data-sharing and battery usage).

I tried both Autosync and DriveSync (AutoSync for Google Drive):

  • ℹ️ Trial-ware. Only get 14 days to test the app before requiring payment. Payment can either by a subscription (yuck) or a single-purchase lifetime license for a single storage provider (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox) (better).
  • ℹ️ Sync's folders between device and storage provider with different methods (two way, upload only, upload then delete, download only, etc.).
  • ⚠️ Need to accept a EULA (license agreement) and privacy policy. It's fine, but a bit weird.
  • ⚠️ Requires "All files access" - bit much, could be using the Storage Access Framework to only give access to specific files or directories.
  • ✅ No account needed with MetaCtrl or Autosync, which is nice.
  • ✅ Simple app design.
  • ✅ Provides good configuration options in Settings for autosync.
  • ⚠️ Some data collected (Personal Info, App info, and performance)
  • ❌ "Device or other IDs" are shared with third parties.
  • ⚠️ Requires turning off battery optimization for the app to ensure it runs "reliably" (or... the developer could put the effort it to ensure reliability even under battery optimization conditions?)
  • ❌ The "DriveSync" version brought up a large "Data preferences" screen after launch to select data gathering preferences for advertising purposes, etc. Many of the toggle options marked "Legitimate interest" (fuck off) were toggled on and required manually going through and toggling them all off, including diving into a "Vendor preferences" submenu (fuck off even more). The regular "Autosync" app did not ask for this, thankfully.

When setting this up, I set it up as a "Synced folder" - syncing my on-Android folder where the Signal backups are made and the Google Drive folder where I want them to be stored. I used sync method "Upload Mirror", to ensure that the folders are kept the same but the uploads occur before any backups are deleted from Google Drive. In the app settings, I set the automatic synchronisation to occur an hour or so after my Signal backups are scheduled. MetaCtrl has a good user guide available for explaining the different "sync methods".

docs.title: My Backup Pro
docs.text:
By Rerware, LLC. Short answer: No - though I didn't even need to download the app to know.

  • ⚠️ Requires payment of 69,00 kr before downloading - didn't want to immediately pay for this, so going to look at the description and available screenshots to evaluate it.
  • ⚠️ Quite an old looking design / interface.
  • ❌ Seems to back up lots of settings, messages, calendars, but not actual folders on the device. Can seem to back up single files, but file-matching configuration is not seem pictured.
  • ❌ Scheduling options are very limited.
  • ✅ Supports backing up to Google Drive (and Rerware servers and Dropbox).
  • ⚠️ Some personal data collected.
  • ✅ No data shared with third parties.
  • ⚠️ No update since 11 September 2023 (2 years!). On one hand, if it ain't broke don't fix it, but also: security patches and general improvements are important.

docs.title: All Backup & Restore
docs.text:
By SuriDevs. Short answer: No.

  • ❌ Doesn't support backing up folders or files. Only: Apps, Contacts, Messages, Call logs and Calendars.
  • ⚠️ Contains ads.
  • ✅ No data collected.
  • ✅ No data shared with third parties.

docs.title: A dedicated app for automations?
docs.text:
Automation software allows the automation of lots of tasks, which could include backups. Looking at the Google Play Store, this is what's available:

  • Automate by LlamaLab
  • IFTTT by IFTTT, Inc
  • Tasker by joaomgcd
  • MacroDroid by ArloSoft

On the Signal subreddit I also saw mentions of the Syncthing, but after searching it on the web, I found this article detailing that the developer is retiring Android support, so I'm not even going to dig into that as an option.

docs.title: Automate
docs.text:
By LlamaLab. Short answer: Maybe, but no.

  • ❌ Very complicated and doesn't have a good UX - even with the flow charts. No easy way to validate, test or just receive feedback that text matching and functions are correct, which doesn't inspire confidence in my written automations. If I wanted to write code to do this, I'd just write my own app. This is not something I could recommend to my family or friends for them to set up their own backups.
  • ❌ When running a continuous backup process, a notification always persists - which is quite annoying.
  • ✅ Seems to support a lot of powerful features and options.
  • ✅ Seems to have a community of people writing and sharing their automations.
  • ⚠️ Personal data collected.
  • ⚠️ Data shared with third parties.

docs.title: IFTTT
docs.text:
By IFTTT, Inc. Short answer: No.

  • ⚠️ Requires an account to use.
  • ⚠️ Doesn't provide a trigger option for "new file created in a folder" - so definitely need to use scheduling.
  • ❌ Doesn't provide an action option to upload/sync matching files or folder from the device to Google Drive.
  • ⚠️ Personal data collected.
  • ✅ No data shared with third parties.

docs.title: Tasker
docs.text:
By joaomgcd. Short answer: Probably, but didn't try and requires payment for use and at least requires some sacrifices on non-functional requirements (data-sharing).

  • ⚠️ Requires payment of 38,00 kr before downloading - didn't want to immediately pay for this, so going to look at the description and available screenshots to evaluate it.
  • ⚠️ Quite an old looking design / interface.
  • ✅ App description on Google Play describes being able to do "Automatic File Backups":
    • "If you set it up to do so, Tasker can automatically back up your files to a specific folder on the device, SD card, USB key or even Google Drive! ..."
  • ⚠️ Personal data collected.
  • ❌ Data shared with third parties.

docs.title: MacroDroid
docs.text:
By ArloSoft. Short answer: No.

  • ⚠️ Contains ads.
  • ⚠️ Doesn't provide a trigger option for "new file created in a folder" - so definitely need to use scheduling.
  • ❌ Doesn't provide an action option to upload/sync matching files or folder from the device to Google Drive.
  • ⚠️ "Pro" as a one time payment (85,00 kr) for unlimited macros and no adverts, backing up macros.
  • ⚠️ Personal data collected.
  • ❌ Data shared with third parties.

docs.title: Watches and Smartwatches
docs.text:
Watches are great because they have very long battery lives (several years or more) and do what they need to: tell you the time. Some watches can even have extra features, without really sacrificing battery life, like: a stopwatch, an alarm, beep on the hour, tell you the date, moon phases.

A smartwatch is one that does even more (gather biometric data, give notifications, track GPS location, pay with contactless, etc.) at the cost of:

  • A more expensive watch - which is not great, but acceptable given the amount of functionality provided.
  • A substantially shorter battery life (several days, maybe a month) - which is understandable, though it might not be acceptable for some (wasn't for me for a long time!), but acceptable for many, given the amount of functionality offered, and that recharging a device is not too inconvenient.
  • Giving all the data gathered from the watch to the company who sold you the watch - which just shouldn't really be a thing, but we accept because... that's how the world works now?

Let's wish for a better smartwatch.

docs.title: Wishes for a better smartwatch
docs.text:
The smartwatch should be able to connect to a "companion app" on a smartphone, and can upload and download information from the companion app.

Smartwatch requirements:

  • Has a long battery life (lasts for years, ideally; months is good; 1 month is OK; several days is unfortunate).
  • Tells the time and date.
  • Tells the weather (now and short-term future (up to 7 days?))
  • Can make a sound and/or vibration at certain times (e.g. an alarm, or on-the-hour signal).
  • Tells other time-related information (moon phases, tides, sunrise, sunset, etc.)
  • Can act as a stopwatch and timer.
  • Gather metrics for different data points:
    • heart rate
    • heart rate rhythm / variability
    • step count
    • GPS location
    • altitude / depth
    • speed / pace
    • temperature (body)
    • temperature (air/surroundings)
    • compass direction
    • barometer (air pressure)
    • blood-oxygen levels
    • etc.
  • Can track "activities" (runs, swims, workouts, etc.)
  • Gives basic tracking / graphed / mapped visualisations for each data point and activities.
  • Can stream locally stored music or FM radio to headphones via secure local connection (e.g. bluetooth), assuming it does not significantly affect battery life (and if it does, then warn the user)
  • Can have different watch faces that offer different amounts or kinds of information.
  • Can share / backup saved settings (alarms, watch faces, etc.) and metrics to the companion app.
  • Can receive phone notifications (provided by the companion app).
  • Is repairable (can replace battery, screen, buttons, strap, etc.)
  • Uses an open source operating system and firmware.

Companion app requirements:

  • More in-depth visualisations and insights into different data points.
  • Download firmware updates for connected smartwatches.
  • Can configure which notifications are sent to the smartwatch.
  • Provides data to the smartwatch that the smartwatch cannot gather itself (e.g. weather data, moon phases, etc.)
  • Is open source and free.

Security & Privacy requirements:

  • The smartwatch does not connect to the internet directly.
  • The smartwatch and companion app communicate frequently (but not so much that ruins battery life) via a secure local connection (e.g. bluetooth)
  • Connecting a smartwatch to a companion app does not automatically share any metrics. Sharing metrics must be "opt-in" and easy to "opt-out" of sharing any and all data points at any time.
  • All metrics must stay on the smartwatch, unless explicitly shared (per data point) with the companion app.
  • All metrics shared to the companion app must be stored securely and be inaccessible to other apps unless access is explicitly granted (and access can be removed at any time).
  • All metrics available in the companion app should not be automatically shared to anywhere unless explicitly configured by the user to do so (e.g. automatically share runs on Strava)
  • All automatic sharing of metrics can easily be limited to specific data points, or stopped completely.
  • All metric data in the companion app or smartwatch should be exportable to a convenient file format (e.g. CSV) if the user wants the raw data.
  • All metric data in the companion app should be exportable to an encrypted backup file for backing up.

Needless features:

  • The smartwatch does not need perform contactless payments, a phone can do that and has better security (e.g. requiring fingerprint before payment)
  • The smartwatch does not need to send or receive messages, a phone can do that with a much better user experience.
  • The smartwatch does not need to take calls, a phone can do that with a much better user experience (and would ruin smartwatch battery life)

docs.title: Sunglasses
docs.text: Sunglasses should fit your face, protect your eyes, be durable, made from sustainable materials, and provide the aesthetic you're looking for.

docs.title: Fit / Sizing
docs.text:
You want your sunglasses to be wide enough on your face so they sit comfortably and not be too tight or too big, and the arms long enough to hook over your ears comfortably.

A lot of sunglasses will usually have sizing numbers on the inside of one of the arms. They look like: 53 □ 18 140. These refer to various measurements in millimeters (mm):

  • Lens width (40mm to 60mm)
  • Bridge width (14-24)
  • Arm / Temple length (120mm to 150mm)

Medium-sized sunglasses are typically around 53 □ 18 140.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Sunglasses should shade your eyes from the sun, but also protect against UV radiation. Amount that sunglasses shade from the sun is up to personal taste, but be careful with very shaded sunglasses when driving.

"UV400" is the recommended protection against UV radiation. This protects against UVA and UVB radiation:

Property UVA UVB UVC Wavelength 315nm to 400nm 280nm to 315nm 100nm to 280nm How bad? Sunburn + some skin cancers Bad sunburn + skin cancer Severe sunburns + skin cancer Absorbed by Earth's atmosphere? Not really Mostly (but not entirely) Completely (Thanks, Earth!)

In Europe, sunglasses should have the CE mark on them, which means they conform with EU health, safety and environment standards - which means they protect against UVA and UVB radiation.

Sunglasses are covered by ISO standards (which have been adopted by the EU): ISO 12311 and ISO 12312.

docs.title: Polarised
docs.text:
Polarisation is simply another way to filter light, specifically by filtering wavelengths that are horizontally oriented.

This is particularly useful for reducing glare from water, which (apparently) can cause sunlight to be reflected horizontally.

LCD screens typically emit polarised light, meaning polarised sunglasses can filter out that light and make it difficult to view and use LCD screens. This can be useful for blocking out LCD advertisements, but otherwise is a slight hindrance.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
Generally, glasses made of stronger materials like metal and decent wood or plastics are durable.

Cheap sunglasses made of flimsy plastic, will be less durable.

Thin arms and frames tend to be an indication of fragility. If you really want thin frames, it's best to keep your sunglasses in a case when not wearing them.

docs.title: Sustainability
docs.text:
Wood, metal and glass are all materials that are either biodegradable or recyclable.

Plastics are obviously not acceptable here - if you are buying plastics, then at try to buy sustainably by purchasing second-hand sunglasses.

Try to repair your sunglasses, instead of replacing them.

When it's time to dispose of your sunglasses, if they are in good condition, consider donating them to a second-hand store, or selling them yourself. If they're broken and beyond repair, break them down into their parts and have them recycled.

docs.title: Aesthetic
docs.text:
There is a lot of recommendations for what sunglasses look best on what faces. Generally speaking:

  • If you have an angular face, then more rounded sunglasses are recommended.
  • If you have a rounder face, more angular / squarer sunglasses are recommended.

This means your features are not accentuated, but softened, making them less jarring aesthetically - unless you want that.

In my opinion, wayfarer-style sunglasses are quite universally "good".

docs.title: Sustainable Hardware
docs.text:
Modern consumerism & capitalism has promoted the following behaviour, when it comes to a lot of consumer technology / hardware:

Buy thing, use thing, {insert reason for throwing thing away}, toss thing. Repeat.

Where the reasons could be: it broke, or you dislike it, or predatory marketing practices convince you that you dislike it or that you need a new one, and so on.

Instead, it's plain better and more sustainable to instead be able to upgrade, modify, and repair the hardware. That's sustainable hardware. That's true ownership of your stuff.

To be able to upgrade, modify and repair your stuff, we need the following:

  • Modular design, to allow for upgrades and modifications to be easier.
  • Be designed to be easy to take apart (e.g. standard screws, non-soldered wire connections, clips and screw-in components rather than glue) to allow for upgrades, modifications and repairs to be easier.
  • Have schematics available for easy troubleshooting, and allowing it to be easy to design modifications or upgrades of your own.
  • Have guides available for how to do upgrades, modifications and repairs.
  • Someone (usually the manufacturer) to provide replacement parts - mainly for repairs.
  • Ideally, publish designs and other technical information as being open source, so that people are free from legal issues when trying to upgrade, modify or repair their stuff, or help others do the same.

Check out iFixit for guides and pointers on how to repair your stuff, and The Repair Association for how to help shape better legislation that promotes the "Right to Repair".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Framework laptop & desktop computers.
  • Fairphone phones, headphones, and earbuds.
  • Open Funk's re:Mix blender.
  • Build your own computer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Everything is ultimately disposable, so it's important for us to use sustainable materials. This means using mostly organic materials, or minerals that can be repaired or recycled easily. Some of these materials include:

  • Cotton
  • Linen
  • Hemp
  • Denim (cotton)
  • Canvas (cotton, linen, hemp)
  • Wool
  • Silk
  • Bamboo
  • Wicker (willow, rattan, reeds, bamboo)
  • Leather, or vegan (apple) leather
  • Cork
  • Natural rubber
  • Metals
  • Wood
  • Glass
  • Natural resin
  • Paper

⚠️ Plastic fabrics produce microplastics (not good) through wear and washing. They also tend to not feel soft or nice to the touch, and can become smelly easily as a lot of them are not antibacterial. Why do companies use them? It's cheap. Don't encourage this behaviour buying or using plastic / synthetic fabrics.

I'm not going to go too much into material engineering, but here's some especially useful things to know:

docs.title: Wool and merino wool is excellent
docs.text:
• Wool aids thermoregulation by the wool fibres forming pockets for air which is insulating and keeps your warm, and helps wicks away sweat effectively which prevents overheating.
  • Wool is antibacterial (prevents growth of bacteria) leading you to not smell for longer, as bacterial growth is what makes you smell.
  • It's an organic material and will degrade well when eventually disposed off.
  • Wool fibres from the outer layer of the wool-producing animal are itchier and typically cheaper. This is good for layers of clothing which won't be in contact with your skin.
  • Wool fibres from the inner layer of the wool-producing animal are softer and typically more expensive. This is good for base layers and clothing that touches your skin.
  • Merino wool is fine (thin), soft, lightweight and slightly stretchy which hugely improves comfort.

docs.title: Sustainable wool
docs.text:
Many manufacturers put the wool fibers through environmentally unfriendly processes before making the wool into clothing to try to make them shrink resistant.

For example the chlorine-Hercosett (aka "superwash") process, the PMS process, the Ozone/Hercosett process or even the oddly-named "Life Fiber Eco-Friendly Treatment". These processes result in the wool fibers being coated in a plastic resin (polymerization) which is not only not sustainable but also somewhat negates the positive effects of using wool (natural, biodegradable fabric and natural antibacterial quality). Other components (like chlorine and ozone) in these processes aren't particularly good for the environment either (harmful to the skin or other organisms).

Some clothing manufacturers, like Dilling or Icebreaker, seem to make decent efforts to use sustainably-sourced, plastic-free or even entirely organic wool. Dilling especially are organic and confirmed (via their Instagram) that they don't use any chlorine or plastic in their production. I contacted Icebreaker and whilst they do highlight their sustainability / transparency efforts, they were unable to confirm what treatments are actually in use - which is, ironically, not very transparent.

I'm not normally a pusher of "brands", as brands shouldn't be trusted, but with the deluge of polyester and other synthetic shit that is being produced, it can be hard to find wool & knitwear brands. My recommendation would be go to a second-hand shop and look in the clothing section, you'll often find some good knitwear there. Then take note of the manufacturers. For example, I've spotted WoolOvers and Aran Crafts. Alternatively, go to a hiking/outdoor store and look for wool clothing and take note, that's how I found Icebreaker. I heard of Dilling via word of mouth.

docs.title: Other useful knowledge
docs.text:
Linen is super light and breathable and thus great for clothing designed for hot climates.

Cork is light, hard but soft enough to be malleable, and often floats.

Leather stretches over time, so if you're getting shoes made from leather start slightly tight to let it stretch to achieve very comfortable fit.

Wood, Metals, Wicker and Glass are good alternatives to hard plastics.

Soft but hardy fabrics like Silk, Denim or Canvas are good alternatives to soft plastics. For items designed to be "disposable" that currently use soft plastics, could instead be paper.

Natural rubber and cork are good alternatives to firm plastics.

Biodegradable bioplastics could be used for items where other more sustainable materials are a poor fit, however some processes for producing bioplastics actually have a higher carbon footprint than plastics made from fossil-fuels.

docs.title: Vinyl Players and Hi-Fi Systems
docs.text:
Vinyl players, also called turntables, record players, gramophones, or phonographs are devices that play vinyl records.

"Hi-Fi systems" is an umbrella term to refer to the various devices that, when used together, can produce records (things like amplifiers or amps, and speakers).

In 2017, I bought a shit vinyl player and was very disappointed with it. I resolved to not do that again and instead do a bunch of research into what made a good vinyl player, and then find an affordable one that met those requirements. I then wanted to pair that with a decent Hi-Fi system that could be used to listen to the records as well as be used as the speaker system whenever I wanted to listen to music on Spotify, or when watching films / TV shows.

Since doing all that, several people have asked my opinion on what makes a good vinyl player & Hi-Fi system. So... why not write that up for anyone / everyone? In fact, you're probably reading this, because you asked me and I pointed you to here!

Now, you could go all audiophile here and buy some very expensive stuff, but that's not the goal. The goal is listen to vinyl records / audio using quality equipment to ensure that the audio is good, the equipment will last a long time, the vinyl player won't damage your records when playing them, and it won't cost you thousands of pounds. Be warned though, that this stuff is a luxury and so won't be cheap. Treat it like an investment in having good audio in your home for the rest of your life.

docs.title: Vinyl Players
docs.text:
First off: Don't just go to a second hand store or Amazon or some other place and buy a cheap or cool-looking vinyl player - not only will it sound terrible, but it will likely damage your records over time and make them sound worse and worse.

Quick overview of the anatomy of a vinyl player:

  • Base - the main body of the vinyl player.
  • Deck - the spinning bit where you place the records for playing.
  • Arm - (aka tonearm) the long bit that extends over the deck, with the "needle" on the end, and with weights on the other end.
  • Needle - (aka stylus) the delicate bit of metal on the end of the arm that touches the record, often part of a "cartridge" piece to allow easy replacing of worn/broken needles without it being too fiddly.
  • Lid - the bit that covers the whole body to protect the vinyl player and record from dust (etc.) whilst playing.
  • Speed switcher - a switch or part of the player that allows you to switch how fast the deck spins.
  • Power switch - Turns the vinyl player on and off, on some vinyl players this might be the same switch as the speed switcher, or might just be a power switch that then starts the vinyl player spinning.
  • Audio output port or cable (e.g. Phono) - the place on vinyl player where the audio signal is output.

The signs of a good vinyl player as follows:

  • When stood, it stands flat, and you can adjust the feet to ensure flatness - this prevents the needle from slipping and possibly damaging the record.
  • Can play at different speeds (usually 33 ⅓ and 45 rpm, and maybe 78 rpm) for playing LPs and single records.
  • Has weights on the arm to adjust for perfect needle contact to ensure quality audio reproduction and minimising damage to the record - you can get neat little bits of card and plastic measurers to help you perfectly balance the arm to ensure the needle is resting too heavily on the record (and doing damage), nor too lightly (leading to slippage) and has a slight bit of tension/weight that pulls the arm inwards, to ensure the needle doesn't slip out of the record groove.
  • A lid to prevent dust collecting on the record and other accidents from resulting in stuff breaking an open/exposed vinyl player.
  • Replaceable needles / cartridges for when needles wear out and so you can repair your vinyl player rather than need to toss it out when the needle wears out.
  • Phono out - many vinyl players try to do too much as an "all in one" solution, but then cheapen out on lots of parts to make it affordable. Skip all of this by just getting a vinyl player that outputs the raw quiet phono signal, that needs to be put through an amplifier (amp) before being output to speakers. This was the case in 2017, but many modern vinyl players may now output an audio signal via USB or that has gone through a pre-amp and is still affordable.
  • If using phono: A ground wire to prevent hum in the audio signal.

When researching for vinyl players with these features, you bump into a lot of brands and recommendations by audiophiles to get specific expensive equipment. Whilst a lot of it is expensive, I eventually found the company Pro-Ject Audio Systems which produces a range of vinyl players with a minimalist look, all the features I wanted, at a reasonable price.

I was lucky enough to find a second-hand Pro-Ject Essential Phono being sold on a local marketplace for about £80 or £100 (2017 on Gumtree).

Note: Buy vinyl records that are in good shape! If you buy scratched and beaten up vinyl records, you'll get a crap sound - so double-check the vinyl record for scratches and scuffs before buying it.

docs.title: Hi-Fi System
docs.text:
Fundamentally, a Hi-Fi system is made up of:

  • Any number of input devices, like vinyl players, DVD players, games consoles, TVs, and radios.
  • An amplifier that can receive these input signals to amplify and adjust the audio quality signal and route the signal to some outputs.
  • Speakers to listen to the audio.
  • Speaker cables to connect the amp to the speakers.

You can get extra devices like equalizers to further adjust the audio signal before or after the amplification, but it's not necessary and decent quality input devices, amplifiers, speaker cables and speakers will produce a very nice sound.

Amplifier needs to have:

  • Enough power (wattage) to drive the speakers
  • Enough inputs as needed (e.g. phono for vinyl player, multiple lines in for devices like TVs, Chromecast Audios, CD players, etc.)
  • Enough outputs for the number of speakers you want (recommend just going stereo, as surround-sound is a bit overrated unless you have a lot of money and really like watching films).
  • Basic Bass & Treble controls.
  • Master volume control.

Speakers need to have:

  • 2x speakers for stereo sound
  • Doesn't blow out speakers at high volume
  • Has a relatively flat audio profile (decent and even lows, mids and highs) at all volume levels.
  • Good size for the space required
  • Durable build quality.
  • A cover for the actual speakers to protect them against dust/debris.

I ended up buying a Yamaha A-S201 amplifier, a pair of Cambridge Audio SX-60 speakers, and 2x 1 metre-long speaker cables from Richer Sounds in Manchester for £308 (2017 pricing).

docs.title: Electric Guitars Overview
docs.text:
Electric guitars make nice noises in different ways and there's a lot of equipment and factors to take into account, especially when attempting to play with a specific "tone".

Typically, noise is made by an electric guitar through:

  • The Electric Guitar producing the raw sound.
  • Various pedals on a pedalboard modifying this sound with effects.
  • The sound is fed into an amplifier & cabinet speaker for amplification.
  • (On a big stage, the cabinet speakers will likely be recorded by a microphone (e.g. SM-57), then fed into a mixing desk and then blasted out of big speakers for the audience to hear better.)

docs.title: Tone
docs.text:
Tone is the noun used to collectively describe the qualities of the guitar sound that you hear, other than the actual note (pitch) of the note. Tone of the signal can be:

  • Clean or Dirty/Boosted/Fuzzy/Overdriven/Distorted/Clipped
  • Bright or Dark
  • Warm or... not.
  • Full or Thin
  • Sustained (how long the note plays for after plucking).
  • Modulated (changed) in different ways.

Many things affect tone - see the other pages for the specific parts to see how they affect tone.

TODO: Expand on definitions/explanations for guitar tone.

Want more help understanding tone? Videos on YouTube can help a lot, for example:

  • Jim Lill
  • JHS Pedals (a retailer)
  • Reverb (a retailer) - e.g. 80s Rock Three Effects
  • Andertons Music Co (a retailer)

docs.title: Amplifiers and Speaker Cabinets
docs.text:
Often shortened to "Amps" and "Cabs".

An amp might just be its own device (sometimes called a "head"), and it then connects to 1 or more speaker cabinets that will produce the sound. "Combo amps" are devices that contain both the amp and speakers in one cabinet-like device - also (unhelpfully) referred to as simply "amps".

From here on out, I'll refer to things as amplifiers, speaker cabinets and combos.

I'll cover the basics of what the devices do below, but to understand how amplifiers and speaker cabinets affect tone, I recommend watching Jim Lill's videos:

  • Tested: Where Does The Tone Come From In A Speaker Cab?
  • This Weird Guitar Cab Was The Secret Sound Of Country Radio
  • Tested: Where Does The Tone Come From In A Guitar Amplifier?

docs.title: Amplifiers
docs.text:
In their most basic form, amplifiers take a signal and amplify it.

Typically, amplifiers can come in three types:

  • Tube amplifiers use vacuum tubes containing electrodes to analogue-ly amplify the guitar signal. This typically produces a "full" (or "warm") tones.
  • Solid-state amplifiers convert the analog signal into a digital one, amplify using electronic circuitry, and convert the signal back into an analog signal for speakers.
  • "Valvestate" amplifiers mainly use solid-state amplification, with an added tube before the solid-state amplification circuitry.

Most amplifiers also apply extra effects, like basic EQ control (bass, middle, treble) and gain controls, which will also affect the tone.

The materials used & build quality is important for durability, especially if you're travelling with an amplifier.

docs.title: Gain vs Volume
docs.text:
Both measure and affect loudness - measured in decibels (dB) - but in slightly different ways.

  • Volume: How loud the output sound is. Increasing volume on will usually simply increase actual perceived volume. This is fed to speakers, where speakers will eventually either break or cause distortion when too loud.

  • Gain: How loud the input sound is. Increasing gain will increase volume but will also likely increase distortion as a loud signal is fed into components and is "clipped".

docs.title: Speaker Cabinets
docs.text:
Speaker cabinets are boxes (or "cabinets") that contain speakers.

They can be bought in different forms that affect tone:

  • Open-backed, close-backed, or partially open.
  • Be large or small.
  • They can contain speakers of different types and sizes.
  • They can have different grills / coverings (which also protect the speakers).

The materials used & build quality is important for durability, especially if you're travelling with a speaker cabinet.

docs.title: Combos
docs.text:
Combos combine amplifiers and speaker cabinets into one device.

This can make buying an amplifier-plus-speaker-cabinet setup more affordable (depending on the combo you buy) and/or more convenient (only one device to haul around).

docs.title: Pedals & Pedalboards
docs.text:
This is a bit of a work in progress... just so you know.

Guitar pedalboards are boards with pedals on them that provide functionality to a guitarist.

Most pedals are "effects pedals", which will change the sound of the guitar that is plugged into the pedal board. Some pedals provide other functionality, like tuning or providing effects for other things that could be available to a guitarist (e.g. a microphone).

For more about what other things (other than pedals) affect the sound of the guitar, I recommend watching Jim Lill's "Tested" videos on YouTube.

docs.title: The Signal Chain
docs.text:
A pedalboard is effectively a chain of pedals. A guitar (which produces the signal when playing) is plugged into the first pedal, which performs some signal processing, before passing the signal to the next pedal, and so on. The last pedal outputs a signal that goes into a guitar amp, that will amplify the sound so it can be heard by audiences.

Different pedals provide different effects, and so the order of the pedals in the signal chain can change how the sound finally appears. Whilst guitars can desire a deliberately uncomfortable tone, it's typically beneficial to stick to a specific order, to ensure the tone of the guitar sound is actually pleasing.

A good order would be:

  • Guitar
  • Tuning
    • Before everything to get the raw guitar tone to maximise tuning accuracy.
  • Dynamics
    • Before all effects to level out the sound ready for further signal processing.
  • Pitch (change the pitch of the signal).
    • After Dynamics, because we want to cleanly pitch shift a levelled signal, not the raw signal.
    • Before all other effects, so pitch shifting can be cleanly achieved.
  • Gain (to adjust gain and/or dirty the signal).
    • After Dynamics + Pitch, because Dynamics + Pitch pedals need a clean signal to work best.
    • Before Modulations, because Gain pedals aren't just about distortion but about increasing loudness in the desired way before modulation effects, since we'll also get loudness after modulations from the amp.
  • Modulations (actual "effects" that make the signal sound cool / weird).
    • After Gain, to receive the signal with the amount of gain desired before modulation effects.
    • Before Time-based, so that time-based effects don't screw with the modulation effects or signal quality.
  • Time-based Modulations (effects that mess with signal timing).
    • After other Modulations, since time-effects can do weird things to signals that make other modulations sound weird if done before.
  • Amp input
  • Amp speaker sound

docs.title: Amp effects loop option
docs.text:
An amp may provide boost option as well as modulation and delay effects.

Based on the order described above, it would be beneficial to insert these effects into the correct points of the signal chain. For this reason, some amps offer the ability to send the signal through an "effects loop" before it returns to the amp for amplification. Amp that do this provide two jack sockets to "send" and "return" the signal.

A send/return effects loop on a "Marshall Valvestate 80V" amp

This results in an order:

  • Guitar
  • Tuning
  • Dynamics
  • Pitch
  • Gain
  • Amp input
  • Amp Gain effects
  • Amp "Send"
  • Modulations
  • Time-based Modulations
  • Amp "Return"
  • Amp speaker sound

docs.title: Pedals
docs.text: TODO: Expand more on different pedal types and how they work.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Pedals that help you tune your instrument by reading the signal.

  • LED / Cent
  • Strobe
  • Accuracy (+/- cent)
  • Mute on switch / pass through
  • Useful to have a buffer here on this, since it's often at the beginning of the signal chain.

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text:
Dynamics == Pedals that "dynamically" affect the volume (amplitude) of the signal.

So: compression pedals. Makes the loud bits quieter and the quiet bits louder to "even out" the volume of the different parts of the signal, before we go mess with it later in the signal chain.

Compression pedals can have a couple of different controls:

  • Threshold (or Sustain, Sensitivity, or just "compression"): Measured in decibels (dB) and it's the amount of volume that is required before the compressor starts to compress the audio.
  • Attack: Measured in milliseconds, this is how quickly the compressor will start doing compression after it receives a burst of signal.
  • Release: Measured in milliseconds, this is how quickly the compressor will stop compressing the audio after compression is no longer needed.
  • Compression Ratio: A ratio of how much compression to perform (1:1 = no compression, 2:1 = some, 4:1 = more, etc.)
  • Volume / Makeup Gain: A extra boost in volume, in case the compressor is compressing as intended but the signal is now a little too quiet.

docs.title: Pitch effects
docs.text:
Pedals that affect the pitch of the sound by modulating the frequency of the signal.

  • Pitch-shifting (re-pitching the guitar sound (e.g. drop-tuning))

docs.title: Gain effects
docs.text:
Pedals that statically affect volume (amplitude) of the signal

Can also take a clean signal and make it "dirty" (add distortion, overdrive, crunch).

  • Gain / Boost (increases gain / volume of a signal)
  • Fuzz (changes the sound to be more of a distorted "fuzzy" tone).
  • Overdrive (increases the gain so that it "soft-clips" to create a distorted tone).
  • Distortion (increases the gain so that it "hard-clips" to create a heavily distorted tone).
  • EQ / Equalizer (adjusts the volume of different frequencies of the signal)

docs.title: Modulation effects
docs.text:
Pedals that modulate (change the frequency or amplitude of the signal) to make the sound weird and/or cool.

  • Tremolo (fluctuates volume)
  • Vibrato (fluctuates pitch)
  • Wah-wah (modifies the signal to make it sound like a voice going "wah" as you press it).

docs.title: Time-based modulation effects
docs.text:
Pedals that modulate (change the frequency or amplitude of the signal) in ways that use time as a factor.

  • Delay / Echo (Plays the note and repeats it on a delay, and the note slowly fades away)
  • Reverb (Makes the signal sound like it's being played in a large echoey hall)
  • Chorus (Makes the guitar sound like multiple guitars by modifying pitch and delay (can sound a bit "seasick"))
  • Phaser
    • Duplicates and modulates the signal with a "filter" and then mixes it back in with the original signal.
    • This puts these two signals "out of phase" with one another.
    • The output is a signal that is missing or altered in a way that sounds similar to Chorus, but different enough to warrant its own effect.
  • Flanger
    • Duplicates the signal, delays the duplicated signal and then mixes it back in with the original signal.
    • The output is a signal that is affected in a similar to a Chorus or Phaser, but is different enough to warrant its own effect.
  • Uni-Vibe
    • A pedal intended to emulate the rotating "Doppler sound" of a Leslie speaker.
    • Is kind of like a phaser, chorus and vibrato put together.

There's a good video on modulation effects by JHS Pedals on YouTube.

docs.title: Buffers
docs.text:
Buffers are features of pedals that ensures the pedal takes in a high impedance signal and outputs a low impedance signal. This is done in an effort to retain signal quality.

It is generally recommended to put a buffer at least at the start and end of your pedalboard ensures your signal strength is maintained between your guitar and your amp, and the clarity of the signal (the notes and tone) are minimally affected by the added impedance of the pedals.

docs.title: Quick science lesson on impedance
docs.text:
Electromagnets produce a magnetic field from an electric current, and changes to the current changes the magnetic field. Variable reluctance sensors (VR sensors) are the opposite: Creating an electric current from a changes in a magnetic field.

Guitar pickups are VR sensors. The magnet in the pickup magnetises the string. Plucking the string changes the magnetic field which produces an electric current. Since the plucking of a string is a wave it produces an alternating current (and therefore also an alternating voltage). The frequency of this alternating electric signal corresponds to the frequency of the note (The "A" above middle C = 440 Hz).

Impedance is a measurement of "opposition to alternating current flow" and can be calculated as:

Impedance = Voltage / Current where we measure the values of an alternating Voltage and Current at the "peaks" of the signal wave.

Therefore, you can perceive impedance in two ways when it comes to electric guitar audio signals:

  1. The measurable output impedance of any device that produces an electric audio signal (e.g. a guitar or pedal output).
  2. The measurable input impedance of any device that receives an electric audio signal (e.g. a pedal input or amp input).

In order for an input device to receive and handle a signal from an output, the impedance needs to match. We as guitarists / sound engineers don't need to do this, as "physics" does this for us by having the input of a device reduce the Voltage or Current amplitude of the signal, to ensure the impedance matches. This is important for handling audio for two reasons:

  1. Different signal frequencies have different measurable impedances (because the ratio between Voltage and Current is different at different frequencies, because "physics").
  2. Audio processing gear produce sound based on the Voltage frequency & amplitude of the signal, not the Current.

This has the nasty effect that if a high impedance signal is fed into a low impedance signal, then for some frequencies the Voltage amplitude will be reduced, which affects the quality of the signal.

In order to retain signal quality, we want to always reduce Current amplitude rather than Voltage, so the audio gear can receive the full amplitude signal. In order to ensure this for all frequencies, we need to ensure that output signals have a much lower impedance than the input of the device that will receive the signal.

A buffer is a feature of a pedal that ensures that the input has a high impedance but the signal is boosted to have a low impedance when it is output of the pedal.

docs.title: Power & Power Supplies
docs.text:
Pedals require power in order to function, which typically comes from a power supply dedicated for powering the pedals (as opposed to powering them directly from mains power).

Powering pedals from mains power, or through a crappy dedicated power supply, or via daisy-chained power cables, can introduce an unpleasant hum to the pedals and effect signal quality, because the power electrical connection is " dirty" (i.e. it carries with it a lot of noise, like distortions, surges, etc.). A good quality power supply can provide each pedal with dedicated power that is "clean" - thus preventing noise from entering the signal chain.

Power supplies can supply different amounts of power for pedals that need power. In electricity, Power = Current x Voltage. Most power supplies provide power for different voltages and currents for different pedals that need different amounts of voltage or current. When connecting a pedal to a power supply, the voltages must match, and the current of the power supply needs to be greater than or equal to the current needed by the pedal. Some power supplies can output configurable amounts of voltage and current - meaning you can buy basically any pedal and then just flick a switch or two on the power supply to ensure the right voltage and current is supplied to the pedal.

Most pedals I've noticed require 9 V and different amounts of current, though usually often under 100 mA. Some pedals require much more current though, like my programmable EQ which requires 9 V and 200 mA of current. Other pedals require more voltage, like the BOSS CP-1X Compressor which requires 18 V and 90 mA of current.

Before buying a power supply, I recommend you spreadsheeting what pedals you are likely to have (or already have and want to power), and see:

  • How many power outputs you need.
  • What voltages you need.
  • What amount of current you need.

and then buy a power supply that is appropriate for your setup. If you want more variability, then buy a configurable power supply, like the Cioks DC7.
