docs.title: 12 Factor App Methodology
docs.text:
Back in 2011, Heroku published a methodology called 12 Factor App, which denotes a methodology for building systems that are portable and resilient.

I've found the 12 factor app methodology to be founded in good solid engineering principles, and with each factor contributing to making applications easier to configure and do operations work.

Below are the 12 factors in the methodology:

docs.title: The Methodology
docs.text: # Factor Description 1 Codebase There should be exactly one codebase for a deployed service with the codebase being used for many deployments. 2 Dependencies All dependencies should be declared, with no implicit reliance on system tools or libraries. 3 Config Configuration that varies between deployments should be stored in the environment. 4 Backing Services All backing services are treated as attached resources and attached and detached by the execution environment. 5 Build, release, run The delivery pipeline should strictly consist of build, release, run. 6 Processes Applications should be deployed as one or more stateless processes with persisted data stored on a backing service. 7 Port binding Self-contained services should make themselves available to other services by specified ports. 8 Concurrency Concurrency is advocated by scaling individual processes. 9 Disposability Fast startup and shutdown are advocated for a more robust and resilient system. 10 Dev/Prod parity All environments should be as similar as possible. 11 Logs Applications should produce logs as event streams and leave the execution environment to aggregate. 12 Admin processes Any needed admin tasks should be kept in source control and packaged with the application.

docs.title: GitOps
docs.text:
Declare config & infrastructure as code and store in Git. Use a deployment system (e.g. Argo CD, Flux, Atlantis) to make what is in the code match what exists in real life.

Usually have some kind of reconciliation involved so that when real life "drifts" from what is defined, then the reconciliation system "fixes" it back to being correct, ideally automatically on a regular interval. (Some CD systems, like Argo CD and Flux, are designed to reconcile/sync by default).

Use cases:

  • Any Kubernetes or Kubernetes-related resources (e.g. Deployments, Services, CronJobs, Istio/Service Mesh config, Prometheus/Metrics-scraper config, Ingress config, etc.)
  • Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, Crossplane (Infra as Kubernetes), CloudFormation, etc.)
  • Component inventory metadata code (e.g. files that contain metadata about applications, libraries, etc. for what is found in different Git repositories). This could be read or deployed by component inventory or visualisation systems.

TODO more on:

  • Advantages
    • Easy to recreate everything from scratch (great for disaster recovery, but also development environment creation, and proving environments can be easily and quickly recreated).
    • Declarative config & infra is nice to maintain, refactor, and work with.
    • Ideally transparent, open to all eyes (internally) and so collaboration on infra & config is easier.
    • Encourages an attitude towards config / infrastructure can be ephemeral/recreatable which makes choosing where you store your state as an easier and more deliberate choice.
      • This combined with my semi-critical take on DLQs means I tend to treat Message Bus/Queues as stateful whilst they have messages but otherwise more like stateless systems, meaning I prefer handling state with databases and having backups, rather than having DLQs and letting messages sit in Buses/Queues for a long time.
    • Easier to handle single source of truth as Configuration that then reconciles (and doing ID/string matching based on standard naming when referencing) rather than treating it as data and building complex event-driven architectures (some event-driven stuff may still be needed for GitOps though, depending on what you're doing).
  • Disadvantages
    • More code to deal with - though this is made substantially easier by fleet management practices (like MR/PR Campaigns, automatic dependency upgrades (Renovate), and other automated code refactoring)
    • Reconciling Stateful infrastructure can be... weird (if there's data involved, and you deleted a thing, you should probably restore rather than recreate? But caches you can just recreate? Or you might need to recreate before you restore? It all depends on the provider and the kind of stateful infrastructure).
    • Reconciling or recreating some infrastructure with some providers has... quirks (e.g. deleting a database might not actually delete it, and so recreating it doesn't actually work, so you need to think a lot about naming and reproducibility of systems more than you would if you were not doing GitOps and just did backups)
  • General opinion: You should be doing it...
  • ...and more than you think. Treating some things as GitOps vs Data, and why you can (and should) be doing it as GitOps (e.g. particularly around IAM configuration - Service Accounts, Access Controls, even Employee User Accounts).
  • Some things to think about when implementing:
    • Labelling deployed config/infrastructure/stuff what Git repo and what commit is currently deployed, to be able to trace back to the code easily.
    • Reconcile the ephemeral / stateless stuff (Deployments, Services, most Kubernetes config, some infrastructure (e.g. networking)).
    • Probably don't auto-reconcile the infrastructure / stateful stuff, but check for drift regularly and alert if drifting.
    • When deploying infrastructure:
      • Plan in branch (block other branch's possible plans), approve/pass checks, trigger apply in branch, block other applies from happening in repo, start apply.
      • If successful apply, merge to trunk to keep in sync.
      • If unsuccessful apply, don't merge to trunk, and re-apply trunk to reset existing infrastructure to match trunk.

docs.title: SLIs, SLOs and SLAs
docs.text:
This document is intended to cover the fundamentals for those starting out with SLIs, SLOs and SLAs.

The Google SRE documentation does a much more in-depth job of coving Service Level Objectives.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: When providing services for use, they likely won't be functional and available 100% of the time. Therefore, it's useful to measure the "level of service" currently provided, set an objective/goals relating to that, and maybe even define an agreement with someone on what "level of service" you will offer.

docs.title: SLIs
docs.text:
SLIs are Service Level Indicators. These are the actual metrics that you measure to define your level of service.

The SLI that you select should reflect aspect of the level of service desired, and not what metrics you happen to have available.

An SLI should have a name reflecting the semantic meaning of the SLI, a defined gauge to state how the SLI is measured, and how often that gauge is evaluated. This clarity in definition makes it easier to implement the indicator and set associated SLOs:

Thing: Measured by gauge, evaluated every time_interval.

For example, an SLI for an HTTP-based web service could be:

Availability: Measured by the percentage of well-formed requests that succeed, evaluated every minute.

Tip: Try to be smart with your SLIs. The consumers of your service likely only care about the level of service when they are actively using your service. By taking advantage of this, you can design good SLIs that tailor themselves to the actual needs of your consumer and grant you opportunities to potentially disrupt your service but not your SLI.

docs.title: SLOs
docs.text:
SLOs are Service Level Objectives. These are the expectations that we set for ourselves based using the SLIs we've already defined. When implemented, it is basically a specific value on the SLI gauge.

SLOs can also contain qualifiers which can give further scope or context about when the SLO is applicable, such as only being applicable during a specific time window (the duration of which must be greater than or equal to the evaluation interval used by the SLI).

SLOs are not "targets" or "goals" for us to achieve eventually, but the expectations of right now. As such, not achieving an SLO should be treated as a serious incident and prioritised accordingly.

Tip: When introducing an SLO for the first time, start by setting the SLO to something that is already being achieved, then plan and develop improvements to the level of service, then change the SLO to reflect new expectations. Setting SLOs too aggressively in the beginning is literally setting unfair expectations and leads to a reactionary way of working that is unpleasant.

docs.title: SLAs
docs.text:
SLAs are Service Level Agreements. These are contracts between you and others on what level of service you will offer.

SLAs are usually made up one or multiple SLOs (that could be more lenient than other internally-used SLOs and/or more tailored to that a specific consumers needs) and detail the consequences when SLOs are not achieved. These consequences are often financial.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Availability is an operational factor in assessing levels of service.

You could think of availability as simply being "uptime" of your service but that massively limits your ability to disrupt your service, since any disruption counts against your availability, even if no consumers of your service were affected. Instead, we can be more selective and consumer-focused when thinking about availability and define it by how much consumers were actually affected.

Our SLI for availability can be defined as:

Availability: Measured by the percentage of well-formed requests that succeed, evaluated every minute.

This means that our availability is only affected when well-formed requests do not succeed. Ill-formed requests that don't succeed don't count against our availability, and neither does our service being offline for any period of time when no well-formed requests are being sent. Evaluating every minute also means that if we have variable usage patterns of our service, we're not

We can define two SLOs could be:

99.99% (aka 4 nines) availability at all times.

An SLA with a consumer of our service could contain a separate SLO that is more targeted to a specific consumer's needs:

99.9% (aka 3 nines) availability between the hours of 09:00 and 17:00 UTC, on weekdays. When this SLO is not met, the service provider will be required to refund 1 month's subscription cost of the offered service.

docs.title: Responsiveness (latency)
docs.text:
Responsiveness is a performance factor in assessing levels of service, usually measured using latency.

We could measure average (mean or median) latency, but latency is difficult to broadly measure, as different service offerings are subject to different factors that can affect latency (e.g. amount of work that needs to be completed, or variability in a query parameters). This means that we typically want to exclude the requests with the longest latency from being included in our measurements, whilst still capturing most of the consumers latency needs.

This is typically done by measuring the percentile in a distribution. For example: the 99th percentile (or P99) - which could be the latency that the bottom 99% of requests achieved (effectively excluding the top 1% of requests that have the longest latencies) over a specific time period.

Our SLI for latency can be defined as:

Responsiveness: Measured by the 99th percentile latency of response latencies in the last minute, evaluated every 1 minute.

This means that all response latencies during a single minute are gathered and form a distribution, from shortest to longest latency, and we measure the slowest latency of the fastest 99% (i.e. excluding the slowest 1%).

Our SLO for responsiveness is then the threshold for what we deem as acceptable latency for example:

100ms of latency.

An SLA with a consumer of our service could then contain:

200ms of latency, during the hours of 09:00 and 17:00 UTC, weekdays. When this SLO is not met, the service provider will be required to refund 1 month's subscription cost of the offered service.

docs.title: Responsiveness Achievability (performant periods)
docs.text:
Sometimes we might not care too much about minute-by-minute responsiveness, but just know how well we achieved that responsiveness over a longer period of time. It's effectively an SLI tracking an SLO for responsiveness (though you might not officially/publicly/contractually have that SLO).

This is achieved through measuring "performant periods", where we assess the fraction of periods (e.g. minutes, hours) in a larger time window (e.g. days, weeks), where service was deemed "performant" - where performance could be assessed if latency (or a percentile of latency) is under a specific threshold (e.g. 100ms).

An SLI for Responsiveness Achievability using performant periods could be:

Responsiveness Achievability: Measured by the fraction of performant minutes (where P99 latency is under 100ms), evaluated every day (every 1440 minutes).

This means all response latencies during a single minute are gathered and form a distribution, from shortest to longest latency, and we measure the slowest latency of the fastest 99% (excluding the slowest 1%). If that latency is less than 100ms, we state that this minute was "performant". The fraction of performant minutes every day is how "performant" our service has been during that day.

SLOs for this SLI are set to the fraction of performant periods required for a service to be deemed "responsive enough" across the evaluation period. Therefore, an SLO for this SLI could then be:

1400 (of 1440) performant minutes.

An SLA with a consumer could be:

1300 (of 1440) performant periods, on weekdays. When this SLO is not met, the service provider will be required to refund 1 month's subscription cost of the offered service.

docs.title: Error Budgets
docs.text:
Error budgets as a concept is effectively "how much of a budget do I have to cause errors" or... "how much can we break things, and everything still OK according to our SLI/SLO/SLAs".

Error budgets can appear in SLIs and SLOs - and so cannot be tied specifically to any one of these concepts.

In an SLI, an error budget can appear when our SLI measures a subset of a dataset. For example, if we measure latency by using the 99th percentile of response latencies over a single minute, we've effectively created an error budget to allow 1% of response latencies in a single minute to take any amount of time (up to infinity). Not all SLIs will have error budgets though, since it all depends on how you define your SLI.

In an SLO, an error budget appears as soon as we set our objective. For example, if we expect 99.9% availability, we've effectively created a 0.1% error budget for ourselves. Another example, if we expect 99.999% availability but only between the hours 09:00 and 10:00, then we have two error budgets: One of 0.001% unavailability between the hours 09:00 to 10:00 (3.6 seconds), and one of 100% unavailability outside of those hours (assuming no other SLOs are set).

We can even set an SLO for our SLOs and create error budgets there, where we might have:

  • An SLI: Availability: Measured by the percentage of well-formed requests that succeed, evaluated every minute.
  • An SLO: 99.9% at all times.
  • An SLO for our SLO: Meeting our Availability SLO 99% of the year.

This effectively means we can breach our SLO 1% of time (per year) which creates an additional error budget.

As you can see, this can get quite complicated, but if you end up defining SLIs and SLOs that contain error budgets, it's a good idea to use those error budgets. This is because sometimes it is much easier to perform a dangerous canary deployment that could break or incur a short period of downtime to do maintenance than it is to do all the work to achieve 100% availability. Essentially: Be practical, and use your error budgets to make your life easier.

docs.text:
Link in with the following concepts:

  • Incident Response Management (i.e. Alerting + Process surrounding alerts + process surrounding issues that weren't picked up by alerts).
  • Business Continuity
  • Disaster Recovery
    • inc. SLI/SLOs: Recovery Point Objective (RPO), Recovery Time Objective (RTO), Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD)
    • Disaster Recovery Plans
      • Basically just large runbooks, but more formalised for disasters, and not regular smaller issues / incidents where normal alerting and process cope just fine.
      • Some of these disasters will be (or should be) the same for many / all systems.
      • Contains things like:
        • Owning Team (Name, Contact Details, Link to on-call schedule)
        • Affected component (Could be a running system, or a platform component, or a 3rd party system)
        • Potential Disasters and Recovery instructions
          • Data loss? e.g. Restore DB Backup.
          • System unavailable? e.g. Rollback latest change.
          • Performance degradation? e.g. Rollback if sudden change, or investigate as a mob.
          • Data leakage or system compromised? e.g. initiate lock-down measures, notify relevant parties, investigate, provide updates.
        • Links to contact details of relevant 3rd parties whose systems this component depends on.
  • Status Pages

docs.title: Organisational Operations Overview
docs.text:
Different organisations work differently, but they ultimately all have functions that need to be fulfilled by some arrangement of organisational operations.

This section of the site covers various topics related to the "organisational operations"-side of software engineering as well as various articles on other organisational operations topics (e.g. administrative functions or management advice).

TODO:

  • Ways of working (Agile, Waterfall, DDD, Mob programming, XP)
    • "Now vs Later?" = Agile, thinking ahead, premature optimisation, architecture, optionality, planning, reactive, think now yes/no, possibly think later easy/hard
  • Decision-making
    • Design by committee vs Design by dictator - no, design with proof, decide by consensus
    • Trade-offs, balance, who gets involved, etc.
    • ADRs
    • Advice and Guidance
    • Facilitating Software Architecture
    • Decision-making processes e.g. ADR processes, Double-diamond design-thinking (problem, solution)
  • Management vs Technical Leadership
  • Hiring
    • What interviews to do (flow chat) - HR screening, Culture/Manager interview, Technical interview, follow-ups, etc. and the logistics involved in each and how the hiring process reflects how you work as a company.
    • What to look for in people culturally and technically.
    • Respect your interviewee's and your employee's time, whilst doing your due diligence (e.g. avoid home assignments unless they are requested, or they are simple, and it's a junior engineer)
    • Technical interview types and what they offer - and how to design new ones when you're unsure.
    • Be relaxed, welcoming, be super clear in the process and how things are structured to set them at ease, make it clear that saying "I don't know" is OK, because not everyone knows everything and learning is part of the job (because it is and the organisation should know that - but if they say it too much it shows lack of knowledge / skill).
    • Be upfront about (broadly) what you're looking for, so they can understand the expectations - and you feel more comfortable asking questions on specifics of those expectations without the interviewee needing to answer the question but also guess on what you're expecting - this removes the guess work on both sides, saves time and makes it easier for organisations and interviewees to evaluate each other.
    • Make sure to cover who the organisation is, how it's structured, what the position is for, and how the organisation works at some point - since this is an evaluation for both parties.
    • Interview signals (body language, wording, when to dive deeper, when to pull back)
  • Management lessons learned
  • Include a "Software Organisation Management Lifecycle" page that tells the story of how an organisation goes from 1 (or few) to a large scale organisation. This would include:
    • What functions an organisation needs to fulfil (Management functions, how workers are organised, how systems are organised).
    • These arrangements are called "operating models", which essentially define how an organisation is structured and whose responsibilities are whose. Different operating models work better for different organisations and their culture and organisational purpose. Aspects of different models have been correlated with and/or cause different effects on the organisation's behaviour (increased efficiency or productivity).
    • How management gets created (what their purpose is)
    • Small organisation model (horizontal slicing for efficiency)
    • Medium organisation model (transition from horizontal to vertical slicing, plus admin departments)
    • Large organisation model (vertical slicing for focus, internally sliced as necessary, plus admin departments)
    • Huge organisations should probably not exist and should just be multiple large organisations (arguably the same for large organisations)
    • Admin departments tend to scale better than product departments.
    • Top-down/bottom-up decision-making/power, and the preferences from each perspective (mgmt, workers)

docs.title: Administrative Functions
docs.text:
Workers do work to achieve the main business of the organisation (healthcare, manufacturing, a service, banking, whatever).

This organisation of workers needs to be organised, and risk mitigated in order to ensure the continuity of the organisation. To do this, organisations need to perform a variety of "functions" to oversee and enable (a.k.a. administrate) the operation of the organisation.

  • We tend to think of management / governance / administration in different "roles"
  • Those roles have multiple functions
  • If we break up the roles into just the pure functions, we can reorganise things differently, and invent different roles.
  • Some roles contain functions that we actually don't want / value
  • As we break up roles and deduce functions, we can classify functions on a Value spectrum (Needed, Wanted, Undesirable, etc.)
  • As organisations ways of working and cultures shift, different functions get moved around (e.g. architecture is getting decentralised more nowadays) - which leaves question as to what roles actually do, and whether they are beneficial.
  • Knowing functions of roles, and being able to reorganise when things change, keeps us well-functioning and may help us avoid bullshit jobs.

Example administrative roles of an organisation that makes software as part of its work, with their breakdown of functions:

  • HR
    • Hiring & Exiting
    • Facilities management (e.g. office management, supplies, safety, renovations, etc.)
    • IT services
    • Employee management tooling (e.g. Intranet, Timesheets)
    • Workplace policy (e.g. Diversity & Inclusion, General Code of Conduct, Work trips)
    • Employee benefits management
  • Legal & Compliance
    • Legal advice
    • Case management
    • Legal / Compliance
    • Auditing / Self-Verification
  • Finances
    • Accounting
    • Insurances
  • Communications & Customer Relations
    • Public Relations
    • Marketing
    • Sales
    • Spinning (i.e. like a spin doctor)
    • Customer Service - Phone lines, email responses, live chat, general feedback.
    • Customer Due-diligence
  • People Management
    • Career development
    • Conflict resolution
    • Continuous iteration of workers' "Ways of Working"
    • Co-ordination / compliance between the team/individuals and the other administrative functions of the company.
  • Technical Leadership
    • Advice & Guidance of technical work in various fields:
      • Engineering Practices (mainly technical but some cross-over with "Ways of Working")
      • System Architecture
      • Data & Insights
      • Security
      • User Experience & UI Design
    • Identifying cross-functional technical issues and driving (facilitating and co-ordinating) initiatives to solve them.
    • Formulating processes and guardrails to ensure high-quality, fast decisions.
  • Business (or Product or Project) Management
    • Prioritisation of work
    • Facilitation and co-ordination of business-focused work
    • Business-work reporting
    • Business projections

I view these administrative functions from a "servant" management/leadership perspective where they have an emphasis on facilitating and ensuring work is done, rather than making decisions on work or being directive/autocratic or engaging in top-down management practices. Workers should be in charge of doing the work and making decisions, but administrative functions organise workers and put processes into place to ensure those decisions and that work is done fairly, legally, is of good-quality, is within budget, is on-time and all workers are happy.

docs.title: Autonomy vs Supervision
docs.text:
Some basic notes:

  • A person is smart, people are dumb.
  • We're all adults, but we've all had colleagues that whine and act like babies
  • We're often capable of self-managing, self-driving and being smart, but we also get distracted by things, value "things we want to do" over "things we need to do", and can ignore rules because we disagree with them.
  • We think ourselves rational, but we often act dumb, irrational and biased
  • Smart rational persons? empower them and get out their way
  • But we are dumb, irrational and biased? we need guidance and limits
  • So we're both. How do we move forward?
  • Regulation and Social contracts give limitations
  • Practices give guidance
  • Science & our Humanity help us refine and improve our regulations and guidance
  • We can learn social contracts to be aware of them and try to overcome them where they are unjust or unfair. The more we understand, the more we can try to adapt and improve our social environments to accommodate for all and be more fair
  • Leaders and Managers facilitate, refine and guide our practices and help us be aware of and adhere to regulation and social contracts
  • Beyond that, we can be independent / autonomous in order to achieve what we're supposed to achieve and what we want to achieve.

Social contracts, link in with different power structures:

  • Formal structure, power is hierarchy
  • Informal structure, power is influence
  • Value Creation structure, power is reputation

Some more in-depth notes:

"I hire people brighter than me, and then I get out of their way" ~ Lee Iaccoca (apparently)

"It doesn’t make sense to hire smart people and tell them what to do; we hire smart people so they can tell us what to do." ~ Steve Jobs (apparently)

Sure, but not everyone is smart and rational. Brigitta Böckeler covers different forms of bias and irrationality. She references Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow book, as well as the Cognitive Bias Codex. We clearly need some guidance and "checks" to ensure we're operating in a way that is fair and appropriate - hence the need for supervision, and the facilitation of that by Management and Leadership.

We also have issues where if we over-decentralise to the point of structurelessness, we would be subject to the Tyranny of Structurelessness, as described by feminist Jo Freeman, where behind an illusion of structurelessness, and unaccountable formal structure actually exists. This aligns with org physics as described by Niels Pflaeging, where formal, informal and value-creations structures all exist no matter what. Combining these theories would imply we need to formalise structure in order to subject them to democratic control / scrutiny, whilst also refining these structures to maximise democracy and value-creation, and further aid balancing autonomy and supervision.

We also can see issues where without supervision / good management & leadership, we have a lot of failures - e.g. boeing airplanes, being built by clowns supervised by monkeys. So we need good smart people, with good management / leadership.

We also need to ensure diversity and fairness in the workplace, otherwise we'll again just be a sea of white men patting each other on the back at the great job we did. We must tackle our biases, and that can't be achieved through structureless autonomy - it requires processes with checks to ensure we're acting fairly - and we to prevent systemic errors, we need to continuously improve those processes.

However, there is some truth to the those statements. Ask any engineer, and they will confirm some management figures have tried to "interfere" and tell them what to do or how to do their jobs, and they don't know what they're talking about - or at least they're well intended, but the act of interference is not appreciated, or it's a hindrance. Because, as we covered in values, we value both the software and the means of creating software - and interference from management is usually not an enjoyable contribution to the means of creating software.

So we need both. We achieve this through alignment.

We decentralise the act of doing work and making decisions, but being aligned through centrally-defined decision-making processes that ensure we're making good decisions. Certain things can be more centralised than others for efficiency improvements, certain things can be more decentralised than others for decoupling improvements.

This aids prevention of problems, without impeding the same hindrances (or level of hindrances) as we have in with more supervision. Though we may need more reactive corrections, if those processes fail us. Too many reactive corrections and our processes aren't good enough. Not enough decisions being made as quickly as they should be, and our processes are too restrictive. Continuous refinement is needed.

We need structures in place that empower us and keep us in check, but we also little structure that gets in our way.

Technical Leadership that acts transparently, and acts as facilitators and guides according to agreed upon values, principles and practices is that structure.

  • Technical Leadership = when established well, engineers treat as "one of us"
  • Transparency = ensures legitimacy and trust in any processes
  • Facilitators = Not dictators, nor powerless engineers, people who help guide the conversation
  • Guides = Provides expertise and knowledge as part of this facilitation, to make sure we don't make stupid mistakes.
  • Agreed upon values, principles and practices = Inclusive-defined and foundationally aligned with other engineers.

Practically this means:

  • Architectural Advice
  • Make decisions transparently (ADRs and an ADR process)
  • Architectural principles
  • Alignment & Standardisation
  • When decisions / desires appear that clash with alignment, re-evaluate alignment to ensure it is fair / just.
  • Fitness functions for existing structure and processes to measure/assess success and fairness.

e.g. architectural advice from Andrew Harmel-Law:

  • Podcast: Architecture Advice Process
  • Article: Decentralised Architecture Advice Process

docs.title: There is always more to learn
docs.text:
Try to learn as much as you can. Not only is learning fun but the gained knowledge and experience is makes you more useful and thus employable.

Often referred to as having a "growth mindset", though I'm not a fan of that because:

  1. Being content with yourself and not "growing" is a perfectly acceptable and healthy way of life.
  2. The evangelism of the term associates "growth" with "good". When the growth term is applied to the economy, it is not always good. If you disagree, I encourage you to go read Less is More by Jason Hickel.

docs.title: Conferences
docs.text:
Going to conferences can be useful. You can learn from others and bring knowledge back to the organisation, as well as network (socially) with other people which can aid business relationships or open up job opportunities.

They are otherwise quite expensive to attend, often filled with not-so-helpful presentations and stalls that are little more than advertising, and are environmentally unfriendly (travel emissions, mass-produced shit "swag", energy-consuming).

I recommend going to smaller and ideally local conferences where the focus is on learning and networking.

Example conferences (many are not great):

  • AWS re:Invent
  • devopsdays
  • Devoxx
  • GitHub Universe
  • GitLab Events
  • GitOps Days
  • Google I/O
  • JFokus

docs.title: Education at work
docs.text:
Learning does not stop after completing a Computer Science degree.

Everyone is constantly learning new things all the time. A lot of people learn in different ways, but I've observed that a lot of engineers people learn by doing, and learn by being taught (often by senior engineers or tech leads, etc.).

As someone who enjoys teaching and software engineering, I've found it odd and often frustrating how little education we provide to software engineers after regular higher education (e.g. a Computer Science degree) and nowadays, there are plenty of software engineers working in the industry without a degree in a software engineering-aligned field.

docs.title: The current state
docs.text:
What tends to happen in the workplace is that we focus on the following:

  • Self-improvement / Self-learning - which puts a lot of onus on individuals to upskill themselves when they might lack the time, skill or circumstances to make that possible, and their career and productivity suffers.
  • Feedback - which is often done poorly (creating deeper insecurities) and even when done well usually focuses more on self-improvement.
  • Learn by exposure - in that people will learn how to do things simply by being exposed to them. This often suffices in order for people to be able to produce code that works, but they often lacks the broad or deeper knowledge or big-picture perspective needed to produce high-quality software and quickly and in a principled but practical manner.
  • Knowledge-sharing between teams - which usually fails due to over-siloing of teams, but also fails when lacking good technical leadership and management to effectively facilitate such knowledge sharing.

We can, and should do better.

docs.title: A few reality checks
docs.text:
First, I think some realities need to be checked, with some clear statements:

  1. Not everyone is a self-starter, and that's OK.
  2. Not everyone will read architecture / patterns books, or management and leadership books / articles, or the latest Martin Fowler posts, or what the latest trendiest methodology is, and that's OK.
  3. A person does not need to have a Computer Science degree (or equivalent) in order to become a software engineer, but it certainly helps.
  4. Not everyone learns by doing, and even those who do can often plateau how much they learn, since "things work".
  5. If we want to see people learn and improve, we must provide them the support and tools needed for them to achieve that.

docs.title: Learning from existing models
docs.text:
We must get better at engineering education, in the workplace.

This reminds me of apprenticeships but more of teaching hospitals - where not only is work carried out, but education is given to future and current professionals in a real setting where they are supervised and supported.

As Wikipedia puts describes teaching hospitals, when speaking of these educational residency programs:

The purpose of these residency programs is to create an environment where new doctors can learn to practice medicine in a safe setting which is supervised by physicians that provide both oversight and education.

Whilst we're not saving lives and curing illnesses and have the possibility of letting people die, I think there's something to learn from this way of approaching education. For doctors, they don't end their education and get an MD and then go into work and start treating people, they go a place where they will treat people under supervision and learn more until they are deemed experienced enough to do so without supervision.

Imagine if an organisation (or every organisation) making software did that for their engineers:

  • Junior software engineers could become more productive and skilled faster.
  • Regular software engineers could become more experienced and knowledgeable faster and need less leadership and supervision.
  • Senior software engineers could spend less time running around trying to keep everybody aligned and instead delegate and trust more, since everyone is more knowledgeable and aligned, and also teach more, to keep the ecosystem alive.

docs.title: Making it happen
docs.text:
Personally, I think there are two blockers to this happening in many organisations:

  • Education is a lower priority and ends up almost never being prioritised.
  • Senior engineers / technical leadership enjoy being smart, and often enjoy showing other people that they're smart, but they don't seem to enjoy (or as much) actively teaching and sharing their experience & knowledge. Maybe it's an ego thing, or a confidence thing, or a job (in)security thing, but the result is voluntary teaching is rare.

The former is a choice, and one I simply must ask people to reconsider. The latter is achievable by either not hiring these overly-egotistical people or making it part of their job responsibility to educate and share knowledge.

Unblocking these two things can spark some initial education where learning takes place. More workshops, sessions and discussions later, and you'll have a growing learning culture.

The goal is to have respectful and continuous education be part of the normal operations of the organisation.

docs.title: Management vs Technical Leadership
docs.text: The two sides to engineering administration.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
• People / Administrative management focused side of engineering (not technical)
  • Hiring, career development, code of conduct, people-conflict resolution, organisational structure in order to ensure workforce effectiveness and efficiency, drives and supports team in their "way of working" stuff (project/team management), access & approvals, aids procurement of tools that would aid engineers in their work.
  • Aids planning efforts by bringing the organisational perspective to planning, creates projections based on statistics/insights gained to aid the organisation project/predict timelines.
  • Auditing regulatory & internal-policy compliance. Communicating with the relevant parties to prioritise the work so that engineering compliance is fulfilled (DORA, system inventories) - collab with Technical Leadership on this.
  • Salary & benefits negotiations, simultaneously:
    • Managing expectations of what is possible to offer
    • Strives meet and improve needs of employees (servant leadership) (though under capitalism, and in for-profit organisations, it is naive to think that managers actually do this - hence: unions)
  • Finds ways to motivate employees:
    • Core: Salary & benefits
    • Material extra: Social spaces & events, funding/resources for learning & development, extra office benefits.
    • Emotional extras: Purpose, Autonomy & Mastery (see: Daniel Pink's writings)
  • Diplomacy throughout
  • Provides advice & guidance to employees to assist them in how they work across the organisation.
  • Different from Technical Leadership as they are expected to know how organisations & people work and how to organise and motivate workers into ensuring work is done, and is not expected to actually know how to do that work or to even do any of it - in fact, doing so can often create internal political animosity, as engineers (workers) usually want high-levels of autonomy and not have management "interfering", and knowing this is part knowing how to motivate workers.

docs.title: Technical Leadership
docs.text:
• Technical advice & Guidance for engineers, makes sure technical things don't fall through the cracks, facilitates high-level architecture, can make final technical decisions where there is conflict.
  • Often (but not solely responsible for): drives initiatives & conversations, identifies new/upcoming non-functional requirements, identifies problematic technical areas that need prioritisation
  • Some organisational structures gives technical leadership more mandate, others require more democracy/process.
  • Existence provides a technical career path and helps prevent flat-hierarchical issues of "why do THEY get to do that and not me?" whilst not necessarily being hierarchical (depending on organisational mandate).
  • Different from Eng Management as they are expected to be technical experts, and are not expected to engage in the people management side of engineering.
  • Essentially, the more senior/experienced facilitators who guide other engineers on how to do good engineering, and be an example of a good engineer.

Software Engineering is more than just a technical effort, it's a social effort as well, where a collection of people come together to do achieve... something, that involves making software. An organisation engaging in the making of software could be referred to as a sociotechnical system.

Management has primarily social and organisationally-supportive responsibilities, and technical leadership has its technical responsibilities but there are a collection of sociotechnical responsibilities that both technical leadership and management must collaborate on. It's basically a venn diagram:

  • A = Technical Leadership responsibilities
  • B = Management responsibilities
  • A intersects B on: Social software engineering operations

Managers can drift into being in roles likes conductors or band leaders (think music). This is a sign management is interjecting too much into technical work, and a sign of weak or non-existent technical leadership (or over-eager technical managers). Technical Leadership are the band leaders / conductors, managers are the roadies & band managers.

Whether its leadership or management, it's important for these people to be present and available for teams. When managers and leaders are stretched, or spending there time away from their team (s), or just not able to make time for the people they're supposed to be leading or managing, then they're not able to engage in effective leadership or management. Absence results in teams losing focus, increase in conflicts, decrease in alignment with organisational goals & conduct, and/or reduces the social cohesion/relationship between workers and leaders & managers.

Inevitably, there will be times when leaders and managers need to "step away" to tend to something else. When this happens it is important to be transparent and open with the team about why this is needed, what is going on and report back on the status of the work - whilst seemingly "boring" and team members may show disinterest in this, being transparent and reporting back continues to maintain a trusting and open relationship with workers. The alternative is not informing workers, which tends to build suspicion into what leaders/managers are up to, and discontent with leaders/managers that they aren't available for teams, and they're prioritising other unknown work.

Further, on transparency, leaders/managers can often view themselves as "shielding" their teams/workers from unpleasant or controversial work (from "above" or from "the side"). The fear here is that the teams/workers would be given undue stress and frustration that the leader/manager can protect the teams/workers from. This is well-intended, but unintuitively the opposite of what good leaders and managers should be doing. By not speaking about the unpleasant work, the workers are not appreciative of the efforts of the leader/manager and, when inevitably the unpleasant work does affect them in an unpleasant way, view the leader/manager as complicit in the presence and manner of the unpleasant work - it also further establishes a culture of "top-down" operation, whereby the leader/manager is paternally "looking after" their team. Instead, it is better to inform and be open with the teams/workers, by describing the nature of the unpleasant work that has appeared, the view that the leader/manager has, the problems and constraints that the organisation faces, and what the leader/manager is going to do about it (the workers may even be able to help by providing feedback, support or suggestions). This builds and maintains trust, solidarity and a transparent and collaborative culture - and if done openly and regularly enough, will discourage this unpleasant work from appearing as everyone would know that information and communication is handled openly that it would be a socially unacceptable to trigger or cause unpleasant work.

docs.title: Contrasting philosophies
docs.text:
I often find engineers / workers, especially seniors or those in Technical Leadership as erring on the side of principles and the "ideal" solution. This can lead to ivory tower architects and out-of-touch principal engineers, but can also lead to inspiring leaders and high quality solutions.

In the same vein, I often find Management and engineers favoured by managers as being more applied to practicality and "realism". This can lead to an unfortunate overfocus on immediate value and poorly-designed solutions, but can also lead to ensuring value is actually continually created and time & money is not wasted.

See also Principles vs Practicality.

Since both of these view points hold value, and both are needed to ensure a high quality vision is paired with a practical approach, I see this as further affirmation that the two "roles" of Technical Leadership and Management should be separate and balanced in power to ensure neither overcomes the other, and each side understands and acknowledges the necessity of the other.

In this, Technical Leaders are idealistic, grounded by realism. Managers are realistic, guided to idealism.

Workers thereby benefit from both support administration structures, by being inspired and supported in the execution of their work, with both philosophies represented and balanced. If workers decide to pursue a career in administration, then both areas are available to them.

docs.title: Remember the purpose
docs.text:
Both Management and Technical Leadership are administrative roles within the operation of the organisation. Different leadership / management styles are talked about in the world, but I tend to finding that "servant leadership"-like styles ensure that the goal of administration function within the company is to ensure the success and happiness of the workers in achieving the goals of the organisation.

In order to do that, they need to be grounded in the workers' perspective and attempt to satisfy the needs of the workers - you need to genuinely care and follow through with that. Too often, Management and/or Technical Leadership shift their focus onto the profitability or maximal efficiency of the organisation, and that leads to culture issues that make Management and/or Technical Leadership's job harder and can result in loss of productivity, people or efficiency (opposite to what was intended).

This collaboratively-written opinion piece does a decent job of voicing the workers' concerns about this sort of need for Management and/or Leadership genuinely caring about the people they're managing / leading.

docs.title: Onboarding
docs.text:
Onboarding should achieve two things:

  • Provide the tooling and access needed for the job.
  • Establish alignment.

Providing the tooling and access are operational tasks usually carried out by managers, IT, HR and other administrative functions of an organisation.

Establishing alignment is to essentially educate the new person in the following areas to get the up to speed with how the organisation functions (the operating model) and the philosophy (values, principles, and practices) and high-level architecture currently present.

The person is usually joining a specific team that will have its own system architecture and team practices. This will have its own onboarding alignment.

Documentation should be readily available, discoverable, mostly centralised and should be the same documentation as everyone else uses - thus forcing documentation to be fit for everyone, is repeatedly referenceable, and doesn't become fragmented.

Onboarding is an excellent opportunity to garner a new perspective on the existing organisation, philosophy, architecture and implemented systems. Whilst achieving good alignment is necessary, it may be that the result is not to align the person to the organisation's philosophy, but have the organisation accommodate or shift from the learnings it gains from the new person's perspective. This can be achieved through regular check-ins or interviews with new people, during and after onboarding and then feedback acted upon by the appropriate people (management, new people, etc.).

docs.title: Operating Models and Communication
docs.text:
Operating Models are the defined way that the organisation "operates". It's the definition of:

  • How people are organised
  • Who is responsible for what
  • How work is expected to be conducted
  • How we communicate and collaborate on that work

All operating models that aren't just "everyone does everything" results the divvying up of responsibilities. This helps people focus on specific areas, but also will inevitably introduce siloing and poor communication / collaboration on other areas.

Choosing an operating model, means choosing how to collaborate and where to silo, and how that siloing is mitigated when boundaries need crossing to achieve a larger goal.

From one perspective, an operating model is just how we're organised, but from another perspective an operating model is just a definition of how we naturally should be communicating with one another. Getting communication right can make the difference between dysfunction and a well-operating organisation.

Things to cover / think about:

  • Different Operating Models and how they affect communication and how work is achieved.
  • The value of transparency, clear communication, and discoverable historic communication, and how to do them well.
  • Communication rules to ensure reduced time wasted on poor communication and increased time spent on good communication and productivity (don't want to have people spending/wasting their days away just messaging people on Slack/Teams/etc. or reading and responding to email - but also want to use these tools effectively to collaborate).
  • When to have meetings and when to not
  • Smallest unit should be a team, not an individual.
    • Emphasises team ownership of work & implemented systems.
    • Reduces / De-emphasises power dynamics.
    • De-emphasises / helps prevent middle-people who are the "bridges" and "shields" between teams, and instead encourages actual team collaboration.
  • Generally, I like servant-leadership and aligned, mostly-autonomous, domain-focused, cross-functional teams.
    • Teams are groups of people who work to serve a particular business domain (or subsection of a domain (e.g. a subdomain, or actual product)).
    • Teams have leaders/managers who provide People management, Product management and Technical leadership needs.
    • Compromises to this way of working are sometimes necessary given budget constraints (e.g. where one software development team needs to serve multiple business operations needs at once).

docs.title: Product Development
docs.text:
a.k.a. product management, or project management, or ... how we go about making software from a "product" point of view (not technical leadership or people management)

Use of the word product here is just to be generic, it could be:

  • Actual manufactured product, that comes with software.
  • Software product.
  • Software service.
  • Other service / offering that is backed by software.

Important things:

  • User / Customer feedback
    • Want low friction, and few people between customer feedback and development team (big chains of bureaucracy leads to feedback loss and poor decision-making / prioritisation)
  • Ideation processes to generate novel ideas (e.g. hackathons, workshops, suggestion box, etc.)
  • Domain-Driven Design (software engineers to work closely with business/domain experts (stream-aligned))
  • Prioritisation of tasks (graph: Impact vs Effort)
    • Low-effort, low-impact? Ignore, unless it's the kind of thing that accumulates into high-impact, high-effort (you want to solve it whilst it's low effort)
    • Low-effort, high-impact? Just do it.
    • High-effort, high-impact? Plan for it and progress iteratively.
    • High-effort, low-impact? Ignore until you have time (monitor impact status to ensure it doesn't get ignored).
  • Iterative development, but don't forget the long-term strategy and non-functional requirements
  • Not all work can be new product development work. Make time for:
    • Maintenance
    • Research & Learning & Knowledge-sharing
    • Revising existing ways of working
    • Reducing Toil
    • Addressing incidents
    • Reducing existing technical debt (though it's often better to not produce technical debt in the first place)
  • Remember: as the product feature set grows, the more there is to maintain. This results in:
    • Costs going up (more to maintain / run) - can be counteracted by attempting cost-cutting measures (though this has its own consequences)
    • Speed of development going down (time needs to be spent maintaining existing product) - can be counter-acted by hiring more or providing better tooling (though this has its own consequences).
  • John Cutler's "Journey to Product Teams" diagram.
  • John Cutler's "Do this ... Not This ... or this will happen" diagram.
  • John Cutler's "Should vs Can" diagram.

docs.title: Resolving Problems
docs.text:
A couple of management's functions are to "resolve systemic problems" and "resolving conflicts between workers".

I've observed different levels of competency at performing these functions and found that a common feature of poor management is to not actually resolve the problem.

Here is some guidance and not only resolving the problem, but resolving it in a way that improves the worker-manager relationship.

When workers speak out about problems, managers must listen and act appropriately.

docs.title: Listening
docs.text:
Workers want to feel listened to and that their concerns are being considered, even if their concerns are invalid, unhelpful, rude or intolerant.

  • If workers feel listened to, then this improves the worker-manager relationship, and makes workers more receptive to feedback (positive and negative) from the manager.
  • If workers does not feel listen to, they tend to feel ignored and debased, and it can seed or grow resentment for management - thus breaking down trust and the worker-manager relationship.
  • If workers feel like they are being silenced, this tends to quickly drive up resentment and frustration, and further break down trust and the worker-manager relationship.

Action is required in order to address the

docs.title: Acting appropriately
docs.text:
If a manager was to not act appropriately, the manager is shirking their responsibility of resolving problems. This can actually be worse in the long-term than not listening, as the worker will later feel betrayed by the manager (because the problem was not solved), which can seed deeper resentment and frustration with management.

In order to determine how to act, a manager must seek an answer the following question:

Is the problem raised a legitimate problem?

I recommend not asking this directly to workers, as they tend to respond defensively and they feel ignored / not listened to.

docs.title: Legitimate problems
docs.text:
For problems that are known to be legitimate, there are a few options to the manager:

  1. Listen, and then address the problem for the worker.
  2. Listen, and team up with the worker to address the problem.
  3. Listen, and empower the worker to solve the problem for themselves.
  4. Listen, but do nothing
  5. Don't listen, and do nothing
  6. Attempt to silence the worker.

As covered above in listening and acting appropriately, options #4, #5 and #6 are quite unacceptable.

Options #1, #2 and #3 are therefore the only acceptable paths forward, and should be adopted. The choice of these options is usually dependent on the problem raised, the ability of the worker, and whether the manager has the time and readiness to solve the problem for the worker.

docs.title: Unknown problems
docs.text:
Some problems are difficult to determine whether they are legitimate or not. In these cases, there are a few options to the manager:

  1. Listen, and inform the worker they'll get back to them - then actually do.
  2. Listen, but do nothing
  3. Don't listen, and do nothing
  4. Attempt to silence the worker.

As covered above in listening and acting appropriately, options #2, #3 and #4 are quite unacceptable.

Option #1 provides an opportunity to buy time for the manager to discover the legitimacy of the problem. When it is confirmed to be legitimate or not, the manager can return to the worker and act appropriately. If the legitimacy of the problem continues to be in question, then the manager should opt for transparency and be honest with the worker and inform them of the reason for the delay, but they are continuing to investigate to ensure that the problem (if it exists) will be resolved.

docs.title: Illegitimate problems
docs.text:
Some problems are illegitimate, and the worker needs to be informed of this. Once again, the manager has a few options:

  1. Listen, and help the worker unpack their problem / perspective.
  2. Listen, and provide information to the worker.
  3. Listen, but do nothing
  4. Don't listen, and do nothing
  5. Attempt to silence the worker / tell them off / outwardly judge the worker.

As covered above in listening and acting appropriately, options #3, #4 and #5 are quite unacceptable. I've included "tell them off" and "outwardly judge the worker" to Option #4, as to the worker, they are often indistinguishable.

Option #1 is for situations where the worker has a problematic perspective and provides an opportunity for the worker to unpack their perspective. As the worker does this, it is helpful to ask nudging questions to prompt and guide the worker to reflect and correct their perspective themselves. If done with compassion, and thus without outward judgement or "telling off", this prevents the worker from feeling defensive which further aids with providing feedback, and it can even prompt thanks from the worker at helping them realise they were in the wrong.

Of course, workers may ultimately simply take a different view to the manager or the organisation. In these cases, the manager should encourage the worker to reflect on their perspective, and reflect themselves on their own perspective (even discuss with other managers or workers to aid this reflection). After a short period of reflection, the worker and manager should reconvene, and if conflict between perspectives still exists, the manager should inform the worker that their perspective is not currently accepted, and they must accept this (sometimes referred to as "disagree and commit").

Option #2 is for situations where the worker has raised an illegitimate problem based on lack of information. In this case the manager is responsible for informing the worker of this information and helping them understand that their problem is not actually a problem (or an unfortunately unsolvable problem). It is a good idea, if choosing this option for the manager to reflect on why the worker didn't have this information in the first place and if there should be some efforts made to improve transparency. Informing workers of this reflection and that they will attempt to be more transparent can further build trust and the worker-manager relationship.

docs.title: Preventing problems
docs.text:
In firefighting, it is better to prevent a fire from happening than fighting one that's already started.

In disease prevention, it is better to prevent the spread of diseases, than it is to cure them.

In management, it is better to prevent problems from happening, than it is to resolve them. Ironically, management are often the cause of problems, through practices like "micromanagement".

To prevent problems, managers should focus more on improving things workers value, especially transparency, inclusivity and trust, and offloading hindering organisational administrative work from workers. Provided these are functioning well, managers should work with workers to experiment with different ways of working to improve organisational alignment, worker happiness, and productivity.

docs.title: Final remarks
docs.text:
As you may have noticed, there is a lot of expectation and responsibility on a manager to act appropriately when problems are raised. Management can be a thankless job, and there are lots of opportunities for management to lose the trust and respect of the workers they manage.

This does not make any of the above less important, but it is also important for workers to recognise this and provide empathy, consideration, and thanks to managers for their good work and efforts.

docs.title: The Rumsfeld Matrix
docs.text:
In 2002, the despicable Donald Rumsfeld said the following:

Reports that say that something hasn't happened are always interesting to me, because as we know, there are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know. But there are also unknown unknowns—the ones we don't know we don't know. And if one looks throughout the history of our country and other free countries, it is the latter category that tends to be the difficult ones.

Known and unknown here refers to two different things:

  • Known/unknown, the noun, for the knowledge (facts / issues / problems) and whether we know the facts.
  • Known/unknown, the adjective, to describe whether we are conscious of having knowledge.

This led to the creation of the following matrix, coined of the "Rumsfeld Matrix":

The Rumsfeld Matrix Known (facts) Unknown (facts) Known (conscious) Known knowns Known unknowns Unknown (unconscious) Unknown knowns Unknown unknowns

docs.title: Known knowns
docs.text:
The facts that we know and are conscious of knowing them. Knowing the facts means we are aware what are risks and what is OK.

The job to do with these is: act appropriately (plan and prioritise).

docs.title: Known unknowns
docs.text:
The facts that we don't know, but we are consciously aware of not knowing about them. Not knowing the facts introduces an increased risk, but be aware that we don't know them means we can work to reduce this risk.

The job to do with these is: Investigate and try to uncover the facts.

docs.title: Unknown knowns
docs.text:
The facts that we know, but we aren't consciously aware of knowing them. They're more intuitive things that are so "obvious" or "common sense" that we don't even think about them any more. This unconsciousness of the facts can be a risk.

The job to do with these is: Try to be aware of them, as they can be subject to (or sourced from) bias. Some will be fine, but some could be creating injustices or unfairness that it would be good to mitigate.

docs.title: Unknown unknowns
docs.text:
The facts that we don't know, and we aren't conscious about them or know they exist. These are naturally high risk, as we cannot directly work to mitigate any issues sourced from them.

The job to do with these is twofold:

  1. Continue to investigate the known unknowns, which will likely help us discover these unknown unknowns and turn them into known unknowns.
  2. Make time for ourselves, outside our regular work, to think about issues (especially the complex, chaotic or systemic ones) where these facts are usually hidden. Without this time and consideration, we get caught up in trying to act on the known (conscious) facts, and we get blindsided by the issues that we never tried to make time to consider.

docs.title: Soft Skills Overview
docs.text:
This is not just being a good person but about the other non-technical / hard skills that are needed in order to successfully navigate the complex structures, processes, and responsibilities that are involved in the sociotechnical activity that is software engineering.

Many of these are transferable to other vocations.

docs.title: Being a Good Person
docs.text:
TODO: Write more / expand on the points

  • Be friendly.
  • Be empathetic.
  • Be accommodating.
  • Be respectful.
  • Hold others to account for their actions and areas of responsibility.
  • Treat people equally / equitably.
  • Follow the rules.
  • Improving oneself.
  • Seek truth, knowledge and wisdom.
  • Prevent injustice.
  • Learn one's lessons.
  • Be comfortable and accepting of failure.
  • Ensure a safe space for the people.
  • Be aware of one's biases and privilege.
  • Aid in fixing systemic issues that allow one's bias and privilege to benefit oneself, or disadvantages / doesn't benefit others.
    • See below on talent & privilege
  • ...
  • Probably a lot of other things.

Generally, be someone who's mostly nice / tolerable to be around, and someone who people want to work with.

I'm trying to not say "moral" here, because then I drift into moral philosophy and I get off-topic.

On talent and privilege:

"I am, somehow, less interested in the weight and convolutions of Einstein’s brain than in the near certainty that people of equal talent have lived and died in cotton fields and sweatshops."

~ Stephen Jay Gould

and:

"Not everyone can become a great artist, but a great artist can come from anywhere."

~ Anton Ego (food critic in Ratatouille, so the line was probably written by Brad Bird)

docs.title: Being Openly Vulnerable
docs.text:
"I'm having hard time."

"I don't know."

"That frustrates me."

"I disagree."

These are all examples of statements that put on in an openly, socially-vulnerable situation.

Being openly vulnerable has it's pros and cons, but I personally believe that it is better to be openly vulnerable (most of the time) than it is to attempt to hide it.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
We're all human. To hide our vulnerability is to pretend / put on facade for others to show that we don't feel vulnerable, which sets a precedent and expectation that other's should do the same. It's already uncomfortable enough to show vulnerability, but with a precedent to hide vulnerability in place it becomes even more uncomfortable to open up to being vulnerable.

If we instead open ourselves up to being vulnerable, then we are usually faced with empathy from other people (not all the time, more on that later). This not helps tackle our feels of vulnerability with compassion and solidarity, but also showcases to everyone else that it's OK to be vulnerable in the social space we find ourselves in. The more it occurs, the safer and more comfortable we feel in the spaces we find ourselves in.

In summary, we hide our vulnerability to avoid discomfort, but in reality, we end up being more comfortable when living a life where express our vulnerability.

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
Some people are dickheads. These people take advantage of vulnerable people and safe spaces to bully, strongman, intimidate or simply manipulate their way into a position of power.

So, the con to being openly vulnerable, is that it opens up opportunities for dickheads to be dickheads. Thankfully, the counter to this is not "don't be vulnerable" but instead: Have courage and actively resist and discourage the behaviour of the dickhead.

It is not often done so openly maliciously, and the dickhead is often not even aware they are being a dickhead. Take care in these situations to not call out accidentally dickhead-ery (it's OK to make mistakes after all) but it is still important to showcase that dickhead-y behaviour is not socially accepted.

docs.title: Being vulnerable
docs.text:
Here's some guidance on how to actively, showcase open vulnerability to help set the precedent for others:

  • When you didn't know something, remark that you didn't know it, and it was pleasant to learn.

    • This indicates to other people that it's OK to not know things, and that learning is a natural part of life and work.

  • When you don't know how to do something, remark that you're unfamiliar with it and that you might need to ask for help, or take a little more time in order to learn how to do it.

    • This expresses truth and reduces the pressure on yourself to show competence in a situation you're not competent at.
    • This also makes it easier to ask for help later, since people already know that you might.

  • When you're giving an opinion, with other people (especially when in a discussion or discourse), use language that shows it is an opinion. For example, try not to omit the phrase "I think..." when giving opinions, or add things like "from my perspective".

    • This ensures that opinions don't come across as facts, when they aren't. This then makes it easier for people to express their own opinions and a discussion to occur, as opposed to others feeling intimidated that your opinion is fact and so become less likely to voice their concern or disagreement.

  • Because things can be misremembered, when sharing knowledge from memory, add clarifications and caveats like "I think that's right", or "I might be misremembering that, but I'm quite sure about it".

    • This provides an opportunity for others to voice their disagreement in case they remember differently, which then provides an opportunity to verify the knowledge if there is disagreement.

  • When you find yourself in disagreement, voice your disagreement politely.

    • This showcases to others that disagreement is OK, and showcases how disagreement should be conducted.

  • When a conversation has finished and there was conflict in the conversation (or if you feel you acted poorly), take a break for a short while (10+ minutes), and then speak to the person you conflicted with to see check in and see if the conflict had been upsetting or otherwise negatively affected them. If it did, apologise and ask for feedback.

    • This showcases that reflection is a good thing to have, and apologising for causing offence is normal.
    • This also ensures any damage to relationships is repaired, and if no damage was caused can further strengthen relationships due to the safety felt in being openly vulnerable.

  • Ask for feedback on your behaviour from people you interact with regularly.

    • This showcases and promotes a feedback culture, and gives an opportunity to receive feedback for self-improvement (to prevent yourself from becoming a dickhead).

docs.title: Preventing dickheads
docs.text:
Watch out for the following behaviour:

  • Being directive / autocratic / instructive.
  • Being overconfident / certain in times of uncertainty.
  • Initiating conflict and being derogatory.
  • Showing a lack of kindness or understanding.
  • Being more focused on "taking action" than on creating a safe space for discussion and consensus.
  • Overriding or dismissing other's opinions.
  • Not providing opportunities for others to help / take on responsibility / offer their advice (thereby centralising and safeguarding their position of power).
  • Not being transparent (especially when prompted) with their intentions.
  • Disregarding others' values and/or seeking to supplant them with their own values through coercive means (e.g. money, bullying, overriding).
  • Being vindictive / spiteful.
  • Intolerant views and behaviour.

Once identified, then attempt to mitigate the issue by standing up to it:

  • Discussing with the dickhead how their behaviour is affecting others.
  • If no empathy or understanding is shown, then make it clear that their behaviour is not accepted.
  • If no change occurs in their behaviour, then action should be taken (depending on the context) to mitigate the behaviour of the dickhead.

It's not intolerant to not tolerant intolerance.

docs.title: Changing the Status Quo
docs.text:
Quite regularly, and not from everyone, I observe a resigned acceptance of the status quo, and disbelief that there's anything we can do about it.

"It's too late to do anything about it now..."

"It is how it is, just accept it..."

"I can't change it..."

"I can't do anything about it..."

"I'm only one person..."

and I can't help but think: "No, it isn't. Yes, you can. Sometimes it only takes one extra person."

docs.title: My perspective
docs.text:
The situations we face, the social structures that exist, the rules and processes we (humans) have created, the conditions we live in, are all things that we can change.

Just because things are the way they are now, does not mean they need to be that way - and if we just decide to do it differently, then we just... can.

Moreover, if we don't change it for the better, the status quo will inevitably be changed by people who seek to profit or gain power for themselves - which usually does not lead to a better situation.

Don't get me wrong, the decision to do it differently can be a frightening one, and the work to make that decision and then implement the change can seem like quite a lot a work. However, every time I've been able to make changes to the status quo, it has always been much less work than most people think and a formalised, empathetic, discussion-based process to making decisions can really make the whole ordeal a lot less frightening.

Even then, it can still be hard work in order to enact some changes, but it's always worth it in the long run.

The hardest part is convincing people that it's possible. People's anchored belief that the status quo cannot be changed leads them actively resist and prevent anyone from even trying.

docs.title: Quotes to think about
docs.text:
I'm reminded of a couple of quotes when thinking about this topic.

From David Graeber, as quoted by Jason Hickel in Less is More, on the topic of debt cancellation - though I'm suggesting to take it abstractly and apply it to any situation / existing structure:

[Debt cancellation] would be salutary not just because it would relieve so much genuine human suffering, but also because it would be our way of reminding ourselves that money is not ineffable, that paying one's debts is not the essence of morality, that all these things are human arrangements and that if democracy is going to mean anything, it is the ability to all agree to arrange things in a different way.

From Yuval Noah Harari, from a conversation with Maria Ressa and Rory Stewart:

I think that more people need to realise that we have to do the hard work ourselves. There is a tendency to assume that we can rely on reality to do the job for us. That if there are people who talk nonsense, who support illogical policies, who ignore the facts, sooner or later, reality will wreak vengeance on them. And this is not the way that history works.

docs.title: Feedback and Appreciation
docs.text:
• Feedback culture is good.
  • Positive feedback (appreciation) is often more effective, but negative/constructive feedback is sometimes required.
  • Showing appreciation is not done enough.
  • Making space and time for feedback to show appreciation and learn for self-improvement helps people feel safe, listened to and improves the workplace.
  • Formal feedback is good, but informal feedback (especially appreciation) is even better.
  • Showing appreciation in the "little ways" is hugely appreciated and impactful
    • e.g. I listened/watched/read/took to that recommendation you gave and I liked it!
  • Consider "Radical Candour" - though sometimes rude or unkind criticism is excused as radical candour - so... do radical candour in a safe environment with people who know what radical candour actually is.

All comes back to basically: People like working with (genuinely) nice people.
